teile.einleitung: Street lamps make paths bright and safe at night. They stand along roads, squares and footpaths. Usually the municipality pays for them with tax money.
wichtigste: Street lamps provide safety at night.
They shine for everyone who is out and about.
Usually the municipality pays for the street lighting.
Often the local electricity company helps to run it.
Modern LED lamps use less electricity.
Too much light at night can disturb animals.

abschnitte.text: Without **street lighting**, many paths would be pitch dark at night. The lamps help drivers, cyclists and pedestrians to get around safely. You can see obstacles and you are seen better yourself. Because everyone benefits from it, the lighting is paid for with **tax money**.

The **municipality** is usually responsible for the lamps on municipal roads. It pays for putting them up, the electricity and the repairs. Often the local **electricity company** looks after running them. On cantonal roads and motorways, the canton or the Confederation is responsible.

Many municipalities are replacing old lamps with **LED lamps**. These use considerably less electricity and last longer. Some lamps are **dimmed** at night or only light up when someone comes past. Some municipalities partly switch off the lighting completely late at night. This saves them money and energy.

Too much artificial light is called **light pollution**. It can disturb **insects**, birds and bats. Also, in bright cities you can hardly see any stars. That is why many municipalities make sure that lamps only shine downwards and are no brighter than necessary.

gewusst: In the past, street lamps were powered by gas and lit by hand.
On a summer night, many insects keep flying around a bright lamp instead of looking for food.

teile.einleitung: The family doctor is the doctor a family usually goes to first. She often knows her patients for a long time. She helps with many illnesses herself or refers you on to a specialist.
wichtigste: The **family doctor** is the first point of contact for health problems.
She often knows the family and its medical history for a long time.
If necessary, she **refers** patients to specialists or to hospital.
For children, the **paediatrician** is often the first point of contact.
In the **family doctor model**, you always go to your family doctor first and pay a lower premium.
In 2014, Swiss voters approved a constitutional article on **family medicine**.

abschnitte.text: The **family doctor** treats many different illnesses, for example colds, stomach ache or small injuries. She does check-ups, measures blood pressure and gives **vaccinations**. Because she has often known you for a long time, she knows which illnesses you had in the past. Her surgery is usually nearby, in your own village or neighbourhood.

The family doctor cannot treat everything herself. If you need a special examination, she **refers** you on, for example to an eye doctor, a skin doctor or to hospital. Afterwards she receives a report and so keeps an overview. That is why the family doctor is sometimes called the **guide** of the health system.

For children and young people, the **paediatrician** is often the first point of contact. She is a specialist in **child and adolescent medicine**. With her there are regular check-ups, at which she looks at whether a child is growing and developing well. She also gives vaccinations and advises parents.

For basic insurance you can choose the **family doctor model**. Then you promise always to go to your own family doctor first when you have a complaint. In return you get a **lower premium**. In an emergency, however, you may go straight to hospital. In many rural areas of Switzerland there is now a shortage of family doctors.

gewusst: On 18 May 2014, the people and the cantons approved a constitutional article on basic medical care and family medicine.
Many family doctors in Switzerland now work in group practices instead of alone.

teile.einleitung: Everyone is ill now and then, for example with a cold or a fever. Then the body above all needs rest so that it can get well.
wichtigste: Anyone who has a fever stays at home and recovers.
That way you do not infect others either.
A fever shows that the body is fighting germs.
Drinking and sleeping a lot help you get well.
If the fever is high or things do not get better, ask the doctor.

abschnitte.text: Normal body temperature is about 37 degrees. If it rises well above that, from about 38 degrees, it is called a **fever**. A fever is a sign that the **immune system** is fighting viruses or bacteria. The higher temperature helps the body do this. But you feel weak and tired.

Anyone who is ill should **stay at home** and rest. **Sleeping** a lot and **drinking** a lot, for example water or tea, helps the body. Light food such as soup often does you good. You leave out exercise and sport until you are healthy again.

Many illnesses are **infectious**. When you cough and sneeze, tiny droplets with germs get into the air. That is why you cough and sneeze into the crook of your elbow and wash your hands often. Anyone who stays at home does not infect other children at school. The parents let the school know that the child is absent.

abschnitte.titel: When to go to the doctor?
abschnitte.text: A mild cold usually passes by itself after a few days. If the fever is very high, there is severe pain or difficulty breathing, or things do not get better after a few days, ask the **doctor**. In small babies, a fever is always a reason to get medical advice. The costs of the visit to the doctor are covered by health insurance.

gewusst: Antibiotics only help against bacteria, not against viruses. Most colds are caused by viruses.
Adults often need a doctor’s certificate for their employer if they are ill for a longer time.

teile.einleitung: Forest paths lead through the woods and are used by foresters, walkers and mountain bikers. After a storm, trees sometimes lie across them. Often the forestry service of the municipality or the canton clears them away.
wichtigste: Around a third of Switzerland’s area is forest.
The forestry service looks after the forest and forest paths.
It is partly paid for with tax money.
Many forests belong to municipalities or citizens’ communities.
On most forest paths you are not allowed to drive a car.

abschnitte.text: Around a **third** of Switzerland’s area is covered with **forest**. It provides wood, is a habitat for many animals and in the mountains protects against **avalanches** and falling rocks. A large part of the forest belongs to municipalities, citizens’ communities or the canton. The rest belongs to private forest owners.

The **forestry service** looks after the forest and the **forest paths**. Foresters and forest workers fell diseased trees, plant young ones and keep the paths clear. After a **storm** they clear away fallen trees. This is paid for partly with **tax money** and partly by selling wood.

In Switzerland you may enter the forest freely. However, you are not allowed to drive cars or motorbikes on most **forest paths**. During forestry work, paths are sometimes closed. You should respect these closures, because falling trees are dangerous.

gewusst: The federal Forest Act states that the forest area of Switzerland must not become smaller.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, every person who lives here must take out insurance with a health insurer. This obligation is called compulsory insurance. It applies to basic insurance and is set out in the Health Insurance Act, KVG for short.
wichtigste: All people who live in Switzerland must have basic insurance.
The obligation has applied since 1996, when the KVG came into force.
Anyone who moves to Switzerland must take out insurance within three months.
The insurance then applies backdated to the date of arrival.
Every health insurer must accept every person into basic insurance.
Supplementary insurance is voluntary.

abschnitte.text: **Compulsory** means: it is an obligation. In Switzerland, every person who lives here must have **basic insurance**, no matter how old they are. That way everyone is insured against illness and accidents. The rules are set out in the **Health Insurance Act**, KVG for short. The law was approved by the people in 1994 and has applied since 1996.

Anyone who moves to Switzerland must take out insurance **within three months** of taking up residence. The insurance then applies **backdated** to the date of arrival. A three-month deadline also applies to newborn babies. You can choose the health insurer yourself. Anyone who does not take out insurance is assigned to an insurer by the **canton**.

In basic insurance, every insurer must **accept every person**. It may not turn anyone down because of age or illness. In basic insurance, all insurers pay for the **same services**. With **supplementary insurance** things are different: it is voluntary, and the insurer may turn down an application.

The **cantons** make sure that everyone is insured. When you move to a municipality, you often have to show that you have health insurance. There are exceptions for some groups, for example for certain people who are adequately insured abroad. The canton decides on such exceptions.

gewusst: Before 1996, health insurance in Switzerland was not compulsory for everyone.
Anyone who does not pay their premiums still remains insured, because the insurer may not cancel basic insurance.

teile.einleitung: The European Health Insurance Card helps if you fall ill on holiday in Europe. In Switzerland it is printed on the back of the insurance card. With it you are treated like the local people in the country you are visiting.
wichtigste: The card is called the **EHIC** for short.
Swiss health insurers print it on the **back of the insurance card**.
It is valid in the countries of the **EU** and the **EFTA**.
You receive medically **necessary** treatment under the conditions of the country you are visiting.
It does not cover **transport back** to Switzerland.
When travelling in Europe you should always carry the card.

abschnitte.text: Every person with basic insurance in Switzerland receives an **insurance card**. On the front is the information for the doctor and pharmacy in Switzerland. On the back, the **European Health Insurance Card** is usually printed. You can recognise it by the stars of the European flag.

The card is valid in all countries of the **European Union** and in the EFTA states Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. Switzerland takes part because it has an agreement with the EU on the **free movement of persons**. In countries outside Europe, for example in the USA, the card does not help.

Anyone who falls ill or has an accident in the country they are visiting receives the medically **necessary services** with the card. You are treated under the same conditions as the local people. If a visit to the doctor costs everyone something there, you also have to pay this share. That is why you should go to a doctor who is part of the state health system.

The card is not a replacement for travel insurance. The costs of **transport back** to Switzerland, for example by air ambulance, are not covered. Planned treatment abroad is not included either. For this there is **travel or supplementary insurance** or a patron membership of a rescue organisation.

gewusst: The card looks similar in all countries so that hospitals can recognise it everywhere.
The card is only valid as long as you are insured with the health insurer. That is why it has an expiry date on it.

teile.einleitung: What you tell a doctor stays secret. This is called medical confidentiality or the doctor’s duty of secrecy. This means you can talk openly about everything that is wrong with you.
wichtigste: Doctors have a duty of secrecy.
They may not pass on what patients confide in them.
Medical confidentiality is protected in the Swiss Criminal Code.
Nursing staff and surgery employees also have to keep quiet.
There are a few exceptions, for example with dangerous infectious diseases.

abschnitte.text: When you visit the doctor, you often talk about personal things. The doctor may not pass this information on to others. This applies to friends, neighbours, the school or the employer. This is called **medical confidentiality** or the **doctor’s duty of secrecy**. It also applies to **nurses**, medical practice assistants and others who work in the surgery.

In Switzerland, **professional secrecy** is set out in the **Criminal Code**. Anyone who breaches it can be punished. Confidentiality protects the **trust** between patient and doctor. Only if you are sure that nothing will get out will you say honestly what is wrong with you. And only then can the doctor help properly.

There are a few exceptions. The patient can **release** the doctor from confidentiality, for example so that she may talk to another doctor. With certain **infectious diseases**, doctors have to inform the authorities so that the disease does not spread. If someone is in great danger, an authority can also release the doctor from confidentiality.

abschnitte.titel: For children and young people too
abschnitte.text: Medical confidentiality also applies to children and young people. Someone who can understand what it is about is said to have **capacity to judge**. Young people with capacity to judge can often decide themselves what the doctor may tell their parents. With younger children, doctors usually talk to the parents. If you are unsure, you can simply ask the doctor who will find out what.

gewusst: Medical confidentiality has a very long tradition. It already appears in the Hippocratic Oath from ancient times.
The duty of secrecy continues even after a patient has died.

teile.einleitung: An emergency call is a phone call with which you get help in a dangerous situation. In Switzerland there are short, free numbers for this. Anyone who knows what to say on the phone can help a lot when it really matters.
wichtigste: The most important emergency numbers are 144, 117, 118 and 1414.
Emergency calls are free, and you do not need any credit on your mobile phone.
On the phone, you first say who you are and where you are.
Then you explain what has happened.
You only hang up when the person on the phone tells you to.
Emergency numbers are only for real emergencies.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are several **emergency numbers**. **144** calls the ambulance service, **117** the police and **118** the fire brigade. **1414** is the number for Rega, which comes by helicopter. **112** is the European emergency number and also works here. All emergency calls are **free**.

On the phone, you first say **who** you are and **where** you are. The helpers need to know where to go. Then you explain **what** has happened and how many people are injured. It helps to know your own **address** by heart. Outdoors you can look out for street signs, house numbers or large buildings nearby.

After the first information, the person on the phone often asks more **questions**. Stay calm and answer as well as you can. They will also tell you what you can do until help arrives. Only hang up when they tell you to. They may need more information later and call back.

Emergency numbers are only for **real emergencies**. Anyone who calls for fun blocks the line. Then the helpers have less time for people who are really in need. Anyone who deliberately raises a false alarm can be punished. But if you have dialled by mistake, stay on the line and say briefly that everything is all right.

gewusst: On most mobile phones you can also make an emergency call when the screen is locked.
The experts at 144 can explain step by step on the phone how to give first aid.

teile.einleitung: Public spending is the money that the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities spend on their tasks. It pays for things that are useful to everyone, for example schools, roads and hospitals. Private things such as your own clothes are paid for by each person themselves.
wichtigste: The state spends money on shared tasks.
Large areas of spending are social security, education, health and transport.
The police, the army and environmental protection also cost money.
Most of the money comes from taxes and charges.
The state does not pay for private things such as clothes or toys.
A budget is approved every year.

abschnitte.text: A large part of tax money goes into **education**. Municipalities and cantons pay for state schools, teachers and school buildings. Cantons and the Confederation finance upper secondary schools, vocational schools and universities such as the ETH. **Research** is supported too. Well-educated people are important for the whole country.

Roads, bridges, tunnels and railway lines are built and maintained with taxes and charges. These **transport routes** are available to everyone. Part of the money comes from charges on petrol and diesel and from the motorway vignette. Public transport by train and bus is also partly financed by the state.

The largest area of spending is **social welfare**. This includes contributions to the AVS and the disability insurance as well as help for people in need. **Health** also costs a lot, for example hospitals and reductions in insurance premiums. Other spending goes on the police, the army, environmental protection and culture.

Every year, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities plan their spending in a **budget**. The parliament or the municipal assembly has to approve it. If the state spends more than it takes in, a **deficit** arises. The Confederation has a **debt brake**: over the years it may not spend more than it takes in. Taxes are there for shared tasks, not for private wishes.

gewusst: The federal debt brake was approved by a large majority of the people in 2001.
In Switzerland, the cantons and municipalities together spend more money than the Confederation.

teile.einleitung: An occupational accident is an accident that happens at work. In Switzerland, all employees are compulsorily insured against this. The employer pays the premium.
wichtigste: An **occupational accident** happens during work or on a business trip.
All employees in Switzerland are insured against occupational accidents.
The premium for occupational accidents is always paid by the employer.
The employer may deduct the premium for **non-occupational accidents** from wages.
**Occupational diseases** are also covered by accident insurance.
The largest accident insurer in Switzerland is **Suva**.

abschnitte.text: An accident is a sudden event from outside that injures the body. If this happens at work, it is called an **occupational accident**. Examples are a fall from a ladder on a building site or a cut in a restaurant kitchen. Accidents on a business trip or during a break at the workplace also count.

In Switzerland, the **Accident Insurance Act** (UVG) sets out who is insured. All employees must be insured by their employer against occupational accidents. Anyone who works at least eight hours a week for the same employer is also insured against **non-occupational accidents**, in other words accidents in their free time. Self-employed people can take out insurance voluntarily.

The premium for **occupational accident insurance** is always paid by the employer. He may not deduct anything from wages for it. The premium for non-occupational accident insurance, on the other hand, may be deducted from wages. On the payslip, this deduction often appears as NBU.

After an accident, accident insurance pays the **treatment costs**, for example the doctor, hospital and therapy. Anyone who cannot work receives a **daily allowance** to replace part of their wages. If there is lasting damage, there may be a pension. There is no deductible or excess here, unlike with health insurance.

It is even better if accidents do not happen at all. That is why there are rules on **workplace safety**. Depending on the job, people wear a helmet, safety goggles, gloves or safety shoes. **Suva** advises companies and shows how to recognise dangers. Accidents must be reported to the employer immediately.

gewusst: Children and young people without a job are insured against accidents through their health insurance.
Suva began its work in 1918.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes there is a dispute with the health insurer, for example about a bill it does not want to pay. Then the health insurance ombudsman can help. It mediates between insured people and insurers free of charge and neutrally.
wichtigste: The health insurance ombudsman helps with disputes with the health insurer.
The advice is free.
It is neutral, so it does not take either side.
It mediates, but cannot make decisions.
Formally, you can also lodge an objection against a decision by the insurer.

abschnitte.text: An **ombudsman** is a neutral office that mediates in disputes. The word **ombudsman** comes from Swedish. The **health insurance ombudsman** deals with problems between insured people and health insurers. It listens to both sides and looks for a solution. Its help is **free**.

You can turn to the ombudsman if the insurer does not pay a bill or something is unclear. It also helps with questions about **changing insurer** or about supplementary insurance. It explains which rules apply. Often a dispute can be settled this way without going to court. However, the ombudsman cannot order the insurer to do anything, it only **mediates**.

If you disagree with a decision by the insurer, you can ask for a written **ruling**. You can lodge an **objection** against it. If that does not help, you can turn to the cantonal **insurance court**. Before taking this route, it is often worth talking to the ombudsman first.

gewusst: An ombudsman cannot decide anything. But it often helps both sides to find a solution.

teile.einleitung: In winter there is often snow and ice on the roads. The winter road service clears them so that everyone can get around safely. It is paid for by the municipality and the canton with taxes.
wichtigste: The winter road service clears snow and spreads grit against black ice.
Municipalities clear municipal roads, cantons clear cantonal roads.
The Confederation is responsible for the national roads.
The winter road service is paid for with taxes.
Homeowners often have to clear the pavement in front of their own house.

abschnitte.text: When it snows, the **snowploughs** set off early in the morning. They push the snow to the side. Against **black ice**, people spread **salt** or **grit**, in other words small stones. This means cars, buses and bikes can travel safely and children can get to school safely.

The **municipality** is responsible for **municipal roads**, and the **canton** for **cantonal roads**. The **motorways**, in other words the national roads, belong to the **Confederation**. All of them pay for the winter road service with **taxes**. The work is done by their own depots or by companies and farmers hired for the job.

In many municipalities, **homeowners** have to clear the pavement in front of their house themselves. Anyone who drives a car in winter needs **winter tyres**. Too much salt harms plants and soil. That is why many municipalities try to spread only as much as necessary.

gewusst: In snowy mountain regions, some pass roads stay completely closed in winter because clearing them would be too much work and too dangerous.

teile.einleitung: A tax deduction is an amount you are allowed to subtract from your income in your tax return. This lowers your taxable income, and you pay less tax. A typical example is payments into pillar 3a.
wichtigste: Deductions reduce the income on which you have to pay tax.
A typical deduction is payments into pillar 3a.
Travel costs to work and the cost of eating out can also be deducted.
Parents may make a child deduction for each child.
Donations to charitable organisations can be deducted up to a limit.
You need receipts for every deduction.
The deductions allowed differ slightly between the Confederation and each canton.

abschnitte.text: With a **tax deduction** you subtract certain expenses from your income. What is left is called **taxable income**, and taxes are only calculated on that. An example: someone who earns 60,000 francs and has 8,000 francs of deductions only pays tax on 52,000 francs. Because of progression, this can bring a noticeable saving.

**Pillar 3a** is voluntary saving for old age. Anyone who works and pays into a pension fund may pay a little over 7,000 francs into pillar 3a each year and deduct it (as of 2025). The money is kept in a special account or in funds and is locked until shortly before retirement. There are exceptions, for example for buying your own flat or starting your own business.

People who work have expenses connected with their job, called **work-related expenses**. These include travel costs to the workplace, such as a train season ticket. Lunch eaten out and the costs of further training can also partly be deducted. For direct federal tax, the deduction for travel costs is limited to a maximum amount.

Families may make a **child deduction** for each child, and childcare costs are also partly deductible. For insurance premiums such as health insurance there is a flat-rate deduction. High medical costs that you have paid yourself can also be deducted if they exceed a certain share of your income. Donations to charitable organisations also lower your taxes.

Collect all your receipts in a folder during the year or take photos of them. The cantons’ tax programs show which deductions are possible and calculate a lot automatically. Even young adults in training can often deduct costs for further training or travel. Anyone who starts pillar 3a early saves tax and builds up money for old age at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Income after all deductions, on which the tax is calculated.
Voluntary, tax-advantaged saving for old age.
Costs you have because of your work, for example for the journey to work.
Fixed amount you may deduct without showing every receipt individually.

gewusst: People who have no pension fund, for example the self-employed, may pay considerably more into pillar 3a.
In some cantons you can even deduct the costs of cycling to work.
A deduction does not save you the whole amount, only the tax that would have been due on that amount.

teile.einleitung: Tooth decay is a disease of the teeth in which holes form. It is very common, but you can protect yourself well against it by brushing your teeth properly and eating little sugar.
wichtigste: Tooth decay means holes in your teeth.
It happens when sugar and bacteria stay on the teeth for a long time.
The bacteria turn sugar into acid, which attacks the tooth enamel.
Brushing your teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste protects them.
Regular check-ups at the dentist help to find tooth decay early.

abschnitte.text: Many **bacteria** live in the mouth. They form a sticky layer on the teeth called **plaque**. When we eat sweet things, the bacteria turn the **sugar into acid**. This acid attacks the hard **tooth enamel**. If this happens again and again, over time a hole forms.

The most important thing is **brushing your teeth**, ideally in the morning and evening with a toothpaste containing **fluoride**. Fluoride makes tooth enamel harder. It is better to eat sweets and have sugary drinks only rarely and not all day long. Water is the best drink for your teeth.

A small hole often does not hurt yet. That is why you go for regular **check-ups**. The dentist removes the decayed part and fills the hole with a **filling**. In many Swiss municipalities there is a **school dental service** that examines children and shows them how to brush properly.

As a rule, the health insurer’s **basic insurance** does not pay for normal dental treatment such as fillings. The family pays for it themselves, unless they have supplementary insurance. That is why prevention is also good for your wallet. Many municipalities support dental care for schoolchildren.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Children have 20 milk teeth, adults up to 32 permanent teeth.

teile.einleitung: A **penalty-free voluntary disclosure** is a way of reporting hidden income or assets to the tax office yourself. Anyone who does this before the authority knows about it pays no fine, once in their life. But the tax must still be paid with interest.
wichtigste: Anyone who hides income or assets is committing tax evasion.
This is normally punished with a fine.
With a voluntary disclosure, you report what was hidden of your own accord.
The authority must not yet know about it.
Once in your life, a voluntary disclosure is penalty-free.
The back tax and default interest must still be paid.

abschnitte.text: In your tax return you must declare all your **income** and **assets**. Anyone who deliberately leaves something out, for example a bank account, pays too little tax. This is called **tax evasion**. If it is discovered, you have to pay the missing taxes and also pay a **fine**.

Anyone who realises their mistake can report themselves to the **tax office**. This is a **voluntary disclosure**. Since 2010, Switzerland has had the **penalty-free voluntary disclosure**. What matters is that the authority does not yet know about the evasion. You must also help honestly to clear everything up.

The penalty-free voluntary disclosure is only available **once in your life**. The first time, there is no fine. Anyone who later hides something again and reports it again gets a lower fine, but no longer goes unpunished. In this way the offer is meant to encourage honesty without people being able to use it again and again.

Even with a penalty-free voluntary disclosure, you must pay the **back tax**. This is the tax that you should really have paid earlier. On top of that comes **default interest**. Back tax can be demanded for several years back, for at most ten years. There is a simplified rule for heirs who discover hidden assets after a death.

gewusst: After the penalty-free voluntary disclosure was introduced, many people reported hidden assets, and the cantons received extra taxes as a result.
Tax evasion and tax fraud are not the same thing: tax fraud involves, for example, forging documents.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has one of the densest networks of hiking trails in the world. Yellow signposts show where the trail goes and how long it takes. Cantons, municipalities and hiking associations look after the trails, partly with tax money.
wichtigste: The Swiss hiking trail network is around 65,000 kilometres long.
Yellow signposts mark the hiking trails.
White, red and white markings show mountain trails.
Cantons, municipalities and hiking associations look after the trails.
Footpaths and hiking trails are set out in the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are around 65,000 kilometres of **hiking trails**. They lead through valleys and forests and over passes. Yellow **signposts** show the destination and the approximate walking time. This makes it easy to find your way even without a map.

A yellow signpost means an ordinary **hiking trail**. If the tip is **white, red and white**, it is a **mountain trail** that requires you to be sure-footed. **White, blue and white** stands for alpine trails, which are very demanding. The colours help you choose a suitable trail.

Footpaths and hiking trails are laid down in the **Federal Constitution**. The **cantons** and **municipalities** are responsible for planning and maintenance. They work closely with the cantonal **hiking trail associations**, whose umbrella organisation is Swiss Hiking Trails. Many volunteers help with the waymarking. Part of the money comes from **taxes**.

gewusst: The yellow signposts have a long tradition and today they look the same throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: After a visit to the doctor or a purchase at the pharmacy, the health insurer sends a benefits statement. It shows what the treatment cost, what the insurer pays and what you have to bear yourself.
wichtigste: The benefits statement shows what the insurer pays and what you bear yourself.
It shows the amount of the bill, the deductible, the excess and the insurer’s share.
If the deductible has not yet been reached, you pay the whole amount yourself.
If the deductible has been reached, you still pay a 10 % excess.
You pay for services that are not insured entirely yourself.

abschnitte.text: The **benefits statement** shows the date of the treatment, who carried it out and how much it cost. Then comes the breakdown: which part is counted towards the **deductible**, how high the **excess** is and which amount the **insurer** covers. From this you can see what you still have to pay yourself or will get back.

The statement says: bill 250, deductible 250, excess 0. This means: the deductible had not yet been reached. The **whole amount** is charged to the deductible, and you pay the 250 francs yourself. In this case the insurer pays nothing, but it notes how much of the deductible has already been used.

Another statement says: bill 1000, deductible 0, excess 100. Here the deductible has **already been reached**. You only pay the excess of 10 %, in other words 100 francs. The insurer covers the remaining **900 francs**.

Sometimes the statement says **“service not insured”**. This means that this treatment or product is not part of basic insurance. The insurer pays nothing towards it, and the amount also does **not count towards the deductible**. Perhaps supplementary insurance will cover part of it.

It is worth checking the statements and keeping them. That way you can see how much of the deductible has already been paid in the year. You can report mistakes to the insurer. Some insurers also show the statements in an app.

gewusst: With “tiers garant”, you first pay the doctor’s bill yourself and get the insurer’s share back afterwards.
With “tiers payant”, the insurer pays directly and then asks for your share of the costs.

teile.einleitung: A vaccination trains the body’s own defences so that they recognise and fight a particular disease more quickly later on. Vaccinations are among the most important inventions in medicine.
wichtigste: A vaccination helps the body protect itself against a disease.
The vaccine shows the defences harmless parts of germs or weakened germs.
Vaccinations are given by a doctor or another trained expert.
The jab only hurts for a moment.
In Switzerland, vaccinations are voluntary.
Basic insurance pays for many vaccinations recommended by the Confederation.

abschnitte.text: Our body has an **immune system**, in other words its own defence against germs. With a vaccination it receives a **vaccine** with harmless parts of germs or weakened germs. In this way the defences learn to recognise the enemy without you becoming really ill. If the real germ comes along later, the body can fight back quickly.

Only **trained experts** may give vaccinations, for example the paediatrician, the family doctor or in some cases pharmacists. Usually a fine needle is used to inject into the upper arm or the thigh. Sometimes the spot becomes a little red or sore afterwards. That passes again after a short time.

Many children are a bit afraid of the injection, and that is completely normal. **Breathing calmly and deeply** helps, as does holding Mum’s or Dad’s hand. You can also look away or think of something nice. The jab only lasts a moment, but the protection lasts a long time.

The Federal Office of Public Health, together with an expert commission, publishes the **Swiss vaccination schedule**. It shows which vaccinations are recommended at which age. Vaccinations are voluntary, and parents decide for their children. Many recommended vaccinations are paid for by the health insurer’s **basic insurance**.

gewusst: The first vaccine was developed by the English doctor Edward Jenner in 1796, against smallpox.
Thanks to vaccination around the world, smallpox has been considered wiped out since 1980.
When many people are vaccinated, this also protects those who cannot be vaccinated themselves.

teile.einleitung: A tax is money that people and companies have to pay to the state without getting anything directly in return. With this money the state pays for things that everyone needs, for example school buildings, roads and hospitals. Even children already pay taxes, such as VAT when they go shopping.
wichtigste: Taxes are sums of money that you have to pay to the state.
Taxes pay for things like a new school building, roads and the police.
Children pay taxes too, for example VAT when shopping.
In Switzerland, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities collect taxes.
There are direct taxes on income and indirect taxes included in the price of goods.
A tax is not a fee, because you do not get anything directly in return.
In Switzerland, the people often decide on new taxes.

abschnitte.text: A **tax** is a compulsory payment to the state. Unlike when you buy something, you do not get anything directly back for it. The money goes into a shared fund from which many tasks are paid. Everyone benefits from this, including people who pay little tax themselves.

abschnitte.titel: What does the state need taxes for?
abschnitte.text: Taxes pay for schools, teachers and new **school buildings**. Roads, bridges, the police, the fire brigade and hospitals are financed with them too. Part goes into social security, for example for people who are ill or poor. Without taxes there would be no public playgrounds, libraries or indoor swimming pools in their current form.

**Direct taxes** are paid on your own income or wealth, and for these you fill in a tax return. **Indirect taxes** are included in the price, for example VAT, the mineral oil tax on petrol or the tobacco tax. There are also fees, for example for the rubbish bag or a passport. For a fee, however, you get a specific service in return, but not for a tax.

In Switzerland there are three levels that collect taxes: the Confederation, the 26 cantons and around 2,100 municipalities. Each municipality uses its **tax multiplier** to decide how high its tax is. That is why people pay different amounts depending on where they live. New taxes or higher tax rates often need the approval of the people at the ballot box.

Taxes have existed for thousands of years: even in ancient Egypt, farmers had to hand over part of their harvest. In the Middle Ages, churches and landlords demanded the **tithe**, in other words a tenth of the harvest. Today taxes are almost always paid in money rather than in grain or livestock. Modern income tax only came about in the 19th and 20th centuries.

begriffe.erklaerung: Compulsory payment to the state without anything directly in return.
Payment for a specific service from the state, for example for a passport.
Number a municipality uses to set the level of its tax.
Charge in the Middle Ages for which you had to hand over a tenth of the harvest.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the population can vote on taxes, which hardly happens in any other country.
The German word for tax, “Steuer”, comes from the Old High German word “stiura”, which means support or help.
Every litre of petrol also contains a large share of tax.

teile.einleitung: With the family doctor model, you promise your health insurer that you will always go to your family doctor first when you have a health problem. In return you get a lower premium. The family doctor knows you well and refers you on to specialists if necessary.
wichtigste: The family doctor model is an alternative insurance model within basic insurance.
You choose a fixed family doctor from a list provided by the health insurer.
When you have a complaint, you always go to this surgery first.
For specialists you usually need a referral.
As a reward, you get a lower premium.
Emergencies are exempt from the model.
The services are the same as in the standard model of basic insurance.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who chooses the **family doctor model** names a **family doctor** as their first point of contact. This person is also called a **gatekeeper**. She decides whether you should go to a specialist, to hospital or to physiotherapy. For this she issues a referral. If you do not stick to the rules, the health insurer can reduce or refuse payments.

Because unnecessary duplicate examinations are avoided, the health system saves money. The health insurer passes this saving on as a **premium discount**. How big the discount is depends on the health insurer and on where you live. The services of basic insurance stay exactly the same. So you do not get less treatment, you just have a fixed route to it.

In an **emergency** you may always go straight to hospital or to the emergency doctor. With many health insurers you may also go to the gynaecologist or the eye doctor without a referral. For children, the paediatrician is often the family doctor. The exact exceptions are set out in each health insurer’s **insurance conditions**. It is worth reading these carefully.

A big advantage is that the family doctor knows your whole **medical history**. She keeps an overview of medicines and examinations. A disadvantage is that you cannot freely choose which doctor you go to. In some rural areas there are also few family doctors, and new patients sometimes have to wait. You can usually change your family doctor, but you have to tell the health insurer.

Since the Health Insurance Act of 1996, health insurers have been allowed to offer these **special forms of insurance**. As well as the family doctor model, there is the Telmed model and HMO practices. Today, the majority of insured people in Switzerland are insured in an alternative model. Fewer and fewer people choose the standard model with a free choice of doctor.

begriffe.erklaerung: Doctor for general medicine whom you see first for most complaints.
Instruction from the family doctor to go to a specialist or to hospital.
Person who decides which treatment is necessary.
Group practice in which several doctors work together and take on the role of family doctor.

gewusst: In 2014, Swiss voters approved a constitutional article to promote family medicine.
HMO stands for “Health Maintenance Organization”, and the model originally comes from the USA.

teile.einleitung: Exercise is good for the whole body. It makes your heart, muscles and bones strong and puts you in a good mood. Children should be active every day, ideally outdoors while playing.
wichtigste: Exercise strengthens the **heart**, **muscles** and **bones**.
Experts recommend at least one hour of exercise a day for children.
Running, climbing, swimming and cycling are good exercise.
Exercise puts you in a good mood and helps you sleep.
Anyone who sits a lot should keep taking breaks to move around.
In Switzerland, the **Youth+Sport** programme promotes sport for children and young people.

abschnitte.titel: What exercise does in the body
abschnitte.text: When you run, your **heart** beats faster and pumps more blood around your body. Over time, this makes the heart stronger. Your **lungs** breathe more deeply. Your **muscles** grow, and your **bones** become stronger. A trained body does not get tired so quickly.

Exercise is not only good for the body. It also helps to reduce stress and to be cheerful. After playing outside, you can often concentrate better at school. Anyone who is active during the day usually falls asleep more easily in the evening.

For children, **playing outdoors** is ideal: running, climbing, jumping, cycling or swimming. Football, dancing or skiing also keep you fit. Experts recommend at least **one hour of exercise a day** for children. It is fine to work up a sweat. The important thing is that it is fun.

At school, doing homework or in front of a screen, you often sit for a long time. This is hard work for the body, especially for your **back**. That is why short exercise breaks are good. You can stand up, stretch or walk a few steps. Walking or cycling to school is also exercise.

In Switzerland there are many **sports clubs**, from gymnastics clubs to football clubs. The federal **Youth+Sport** programme supports courses and camps for children and young people. **PE lessons** at school are also part of it. People who exercise regularly fall ill less often, and that also helps to keep health costs low.

gewusst: The heart is a muscle and becomes stronger through training, just like the leg muscles.
Youth+Sport has existed in Switzerland since 1972.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, every person pays a premium for health insurance. How high it is also depends on age. The law has three age groups for this.
wichtigste: The Health Insurance Act, KVG, has three premium categories.
Children are 0 to 18 years old.
Young adults are 19 to 25 years old.
Adults are 26 years old and older.
Children pay the lowest premiums, and young adults usually pay less than adults.
The premium also depends on where you live and on the deductible.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, **basic insurance** is compulsory for everyone. This is set out in the **Health Insurance Act**, **KVG** for short. It divides insured people into three **premium categories**: **children** from 0 to 18, **young adults** from 19 to 25 and **adults** from 26. Within one group, everyone with the same insurer in the same place pays the same amount, whether they are healthy or ill.

**Children** have the lowest premiums. Families often get extra discounts if several children are with the same insurer. **Young adults** usually pay less than adults, because many of them are still in education or training. **Adults** pay the highest premiums. People who earn little can get a **premium reduction** from the canton.

The premium does not depend on age alone. **Where you live** is also important, because there are different **premium regions**. You also choose a **deductible**. This is the amount you pay yourself each year before the insurer pays. For children it starts at 0 francs, and for adults at 300 francs. A higher deductible makes the premium cheaper.

Your group does not change straight away on your birthday. The change always happens at the start of the following year. So anyone who turns 19 pays the premium for young adults from the next January. The same applies to the change at 26. That is why it is worth comparing insurers’ premiums at this age.

gewusst: Premiums are announced every autumn for the following year.
Children also pay less for the excess: their yearly maximum is half as high as for adults.

teile.einleitung: The residence principle determines where you pay taxes in Switzerland. What counts is the place where you live, not the place where you work. That is where you pay income and wealth taxes.
wichtigste: You pay income and wealth taxes where you live.
The place where you work generally plays no part in this.
Your residence for tax purposes is where the centre of your life is.
For houses and land, you also pay tax where they are located.
Special rules apply to cross-border commuters.

abschnitte.text: Under the **residence principle**, you pay **income and wealth tax** in the municipality and the canton where you live. So someone who lives in Zug and works in Zurich pays tax in Zug. The **place of work** generally plays no part. This also applies to people who commute a long way every day.

Your **residence for tax purposes** is where the **centre of your life** is. Usually this is the place where you are registered and live with your family. Anyone who has a holiday flat does not have their residence there. If it is unclear, what decides is where you spend most of your time and where your closest ties are.

If someone owns a **house** or a piece of land in another canton, this part is taxed where it is located. For **cross-border commuters** who live abroad and work in Switzerland, there are special agreements with the neighbouring countries. Foreign workers without a settlement permit often pay **withholding tax**, which is deducted directly from their wages.

gewusst: So that nobody is taxed twice, the Federal Constitution forbids double taxation between cantons.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who does further training for their job is investing in their knowledge. The state supports this by letting you deduct the costs in your tax return. Hobby courses, however, do not count.
wichtigste: Costs for job-related education and further training are deductible.
These include, for example, course fees and learning materials.
The deduction is limited to a maximum amount.
This rule has applied to the Confederation and the cantons since 2016.
Courses just for a hobby cannot be deducted.

abschnitte.text: Costs for **job-related** education and further training are deductible. This might be, for example, a language course for work, a computer course or training to become a specialist. This includes **course fees**, **learning materials** and often also travel costs to the place where the course is held. It is important that the further training is useful for the job.

The deduction is **limited**. For **direct federal tax** there has been a fixed maximum amount per year since 2016. The cantons set their own maximum amounts. If the employer pays for the course, you may not deduct it yourself.

A guitar course or a cookery course for your free time is a **hobby expense**. Costs like these cannot be deducted. But anyone who wants to become a chef and attends a course for this can deduct it. So it depends on why you are doing the course.

gewusst: Basic education, for example your first apprenticeship or upper secondary school, is not part of the further training deduction.

teile.einleitung: Every day we come into contact with germs. Even so, we only rarely get ill. We owe this to our immune defences, the immune system.
wichtigste: Immune defences protect the body from illnesses.
The body’s defence system is called the immune system.
White blood cells fight germs that cause disease.
Skin and mucous membranes keep out many germs.
Eating healthily, getting enough sleep and exercise strengthen your defences.
Vaccinations train the immune system.

abschnitte.text: All around us there are **germs that cause disease**, for example **viruses** and **bacteria**. The body has its own defence system against them: the **immune system**. Its strength is called our **immune defences**. The first protective wall is the **skin** and the **mucous membranes** in the nose and mouth. They keep out many germs before they get into the body.

abschnitte.titel: The defence troops in the blood
abschnitte.text: If germs still get into the body, the **white blood cells** come into action. Some simply eat up germs. Others make **antibodies**. These are substances that fit one particular germ exactly and make it harmless. The immune system remembers germs. If the same germ comes back later, it can react faster.

When we are ill, we sometimes get a **fever**. Our body temperature then rises above about 38 degrees. This is unpleasant, but often helps the body. Many germs do not like the heat, and the defences work faster. If the fever is very high or lasts a long time, you should go to the doctor.

You can do a lot to help your immune defences work well. **Healthy food** with fruit and vegetables, enough **sleep** and **exercise** in the fresh air are important. **Vaccinations** help too. They show the immune system a harmless part of a germ so that it recognises it later. In Switzerland, health insurance pays for many vaccinations for children.

gewusst: A large part of the immune system is in the gut.
Tears also contain substances that fight bacteria.

teile.einleitung: Tax is not calculated on your whole wage. First you may make permitted **deductions**. What is left afterwards is called **taxable income**, and the tax is calculated on that.
wichtigste: First you add up all your income, for example wages and interest.
From this you subtract the permitted deductions.
What is left is your taxable income.
Income tax is calculated on this amount.
Typical deductions are work expenses, insurance premiums and payments into pillar 3a.
The lower your taxable income, the less tax you pay.

abschnitte.text: At the start is your **total income**. This includes the **wages** from your salary statement, but also **interest** on your savings account, a pension or earnings from a side job. You write all of this in your **tax return**. Together it gives the sum of all your income.

You may subtract certain amounts from your total income. These are the **deductions**. They include **work expenses** such as the journey to work or meals eaten away from home. **Health insurance premiums** up to a maximum amount and payments into **pillar 3a** can also be deducted. Parents also get a **child deduction**.

Income minus deductions gives your **taxable income**. The tax office applies the **tax scale** to this amount. The deductions may differ slightly between the Confederation, the canton and the municipality. That is why the tax bill sometimes does not show the same figure everywhere.

In Switzerland the tax rate rises with income. This is called **progression**. If you declare deductions correctly, you lower your taxable income and therefore pay less. It is important only to make genuine deductions and to keep the **receipts**. The tax office can ask for them.

gewusst: As well as taxable income there is also taxable wealth, on which wealth tax is calculated.
People who earn little sometimes have a taxable income of zero francs after deductions.

teile.einleitung: You can also fall ill or have an accident on holiday. Swiss basic insurance then helps abroad, but not equally everywhere. That is why it is worth checking your own insurance before a trip.
wichtigste: Abroad, basic insurance only pays for emergencies, not for planned treatment.
In the EU and EFTA, you are treated like the insured people in the country you are visiting.
For this you need the European Health Insurance Card on the back of your insurance card.
Outside the EU and EFTA, basic insurance pays at most twice the costs in Switzerland.
In countries such as the USA, this is often not enough, because treatment there is very expensive.
Travel insurance or supplementary insurance can close the gap.

abschnitte.text: Abroad, **basic insurance** only pays for **emergency treatment**. This is treatment that cannot wait until you return to Switzerland. Anyone who travels abroad specially to be treated does not normally get this paid for. The deductible and excess also apply abroad.

In the countries of the **EU** and **EFTA**, you are treated like the insured people in the country you are visiting. For this you show the **European Health Insurance Card**. With most insurers it is on the back of the insurance card. It is best to go to doctors or hospitals that work with the country’s state system. Private clinics can cost more.

Outside the EU and EFTA, basic insurance pays at most **twice** what the treatment would have cost in Switzerland. In countries such as the **USA**, treatment is often much more expensive. Then a large part of the bill remains unpaid. That is why **travel insurance** or suitable supplementary insurance is important for long-distance travel. Transport back to Switzerland is usually not covered by basic insurance.

Before the trip, check which **insurance** you have. The insurance card belongs in your luggage, as does the emergency number of your own health insurer. In an emergency, contact the insurer or the travel insurance as early as possible. Keep bills and reports from abroad safe. You submit them to the insurer later.

gewusst: The European Health Insurance Card is often already printed on the back of the normal insurance card.
Rega uses its own air ambulance jets to bring sick or injured people back to Switzerland from abroad.

teile.einleitung: Taxes have to be paid by a certain date. Anyone who pays late has to pay default interest on top. If the taxes remain completely unpaid, debt enforcement proceedings can follow.
wichtigste: Every tax bill has a due date.
Anyone who pays after that owes default interest.
The interest rate is set by the Confederation and the cantons.
If taxes remain unpaid, the tax office can start debt enforcement proceedings.
Anyone who cannot pay should talk to the tax office early.

abschnitte.text: Every tax bill states the date by which it has to be paid. This is the **due date**. Anyone who pays after that has to pay **default interest**. This is an extra amount because the state had to wait longer for its money. The interest rate is set by the Confederation and the cantons.

If someone still does not pay, the tax office sends a **reminder**. If the bill remains unpaid, it can start **debt enforcement proceedings** at the **debt enforcement office**. Debt enforcement is entered in the debt enforcement register. This can cause disadvantages later, for example when looking for a flat.

Anyone who cannot pay everything at once should contact the **tax office** early. Often a **payment plan** is possible. In cases of hardship you can also ask for tax remission. Budget advice services can also help.

gewusst: The other way round, in many cantons anyone who pays their taxes earlier than necessary receives a little credit interest.

teile.einleitung: Cooling is simple first aid for bumps, bruises, insect stings or small burns. Cold relieves pain and helps an area swell up less.
wichtigste: Cooling helps a bump swell up less.
You never put ice or an ice pack directly on the skin, but wrap it in a cloth.
You cool with short breaks so that the skin does not freeze.
Small burns are cooled with running water that is not ice-cold.
With a serious head injury, you call for help.

abschnitte.text: When you knock yourself, small blood vessels are injured. Blood and fluid collect under the skin, and a **bump** or a bruise forms. **Cold** makes the blood vessels contract. This means less fluid leaks out, the **swelling** stays smaller and the pain eases.

You put an **ice pack**, ice cubes or something cold from the freezer **in a cloth** and hold it on the spot. Ice directly on the skin can damage it. After a few minutes you take a short break. A cold, wet flannel also helps. With sports injuries, you also raise the injured leg or arm.

If you have burnt yourself on a hot pan, hold the spot under **running water** straight away. The water should be cool, but not ice-cold. Keep cooling it like this for a few minutes. For large burns or with small children, get medical help.

abschnitte.titel: When to go to the doctor?
abschnitte.text: A small bump on the head is usually harmless. But if you feel dizzy, sick or very tired after a fall, you must go to the **doctor**. If someone vomits or has a bad headache, also get help, in an emergency on the number **144**. Adults keep an eye on a child for a while after a knock to the head.

gewusst: A bag of frozen vegetables can also be used as an ice pack.
A bruise turns green and yellow over time, because the body breaks down the blood.

teile.einleitung: A doctor is an expert who recognises and treats illnesses and injuries. When you are ill and need help, you go to the doctor. In Switzerland, the family doctor is often the first point of contact for all health questions.
wichtigste: Anyone who is ill and needs help goes to the doctor.
Doctors study medicine at a university for six years.
After that comes several years of further training to become a specialist.
The family doctor is usually the first point of contact.
For children and young people there are paediatricians.
Visits to the doctor are billed through health insurance.
In an emergency in Switzerland, you dial 144.

abschnitte.text: Doctors examine people, find out what they are suffering from and treat them. Recognising an illness is called a **diagnosis**. To do this, they listen to the heart and lungs with a **stethoscope**, for example, take your temperature or do blood tests. Then they prescribe medicines, give advice or refer you to a specialist.

The **family doctor** often knows her patients for many years. She treats common illnesses such as flu, earache or small injuries. For special problems she sends you to a **specialist**, for example an eye doctor, a skin doctor or a heart specialist. Children and young people usually go to a paediatrician, who specialises in young people.

In Switzerland, studying medicine takes six years, for example at the universities of Zurich, Bern, Basel, Geneva or Lausanne. Because there are many more interested people than university places, many cantons have to hold an **aptitude test**. After studying comes the federal state examination. Then young doctors usually work in hospital for five to six years until they become specialists.

Anyone who goes to a surgery shows their health insurance **insurance card**. The doctor bills her services according to a nationwide **tariff**, which gives every activity a value. Depending on the insurer, the bill goes directly to the health insurance fund or first to the patient. You pay part of the costs yourself through the deductible and the excess, but for children the deductible is often zero francs.

In a life-threatening emergency, you immediately call **144** for an ambulance. Outside surgery opening hours there is an emergency doctor service in every region. Many health insurers also offer telephone advice, where experts assess how urgent a problem is. For serious cases there is the emergency department at the hospital.

The famous doctor **Hippocrates**, who is considered the father of medicine, lived in ancient Greece. The oath named after him obliges doctors to help the sick and not to harm them. Today many doctors make a modern promise that is based on this oath. Doctors are also bound by **medical confidentiality** and may not tell anyone anything about their patients.

begriffe.erklaerung: Finding out which illness someone has.
Listening device with which you can listen to the heart and lungs.
Doctor with extra training for a particular area, for example the eyes.
The doctor’s duty not to tell anyone anything about their patients.

gewusst: More than 40,000 doctors work in Switzerland (as of 2023).
For some years now, more women than men have been starting to study medicine in Switzerland.
Doctors also have to keep training throughout their lives to stay up to date.

teile.einleitung: In physiotherapy you learn to move well again after an injury or when you are in pain. A physiotherapist shows you suitable exercises for this. If a doctor prescribes the therapy, basic insurance helps to pay.
wichtigste: Physiotherapy helps you to move well again after an injury.
The physiotherapist shows you exercises for muscles and joints.
Basic insurance pays if a doctor has prescribed it.
The deductible and excess also apply to physiotherapy.
Each prescription is for a certain number of sessions.
Continuing to practise at home is important for success.

abschnitte.text: **Physiotherapy** helps people to move well again. This is important after an accident, after an operation or with back pain. The **physiotherapist** first examines what is not working well. Then she puts together a programme of suitable **exercises**. These make muscles and joints strong and flexible again.

In a session you mainly do **exercises**, often with balls, bands or equipment. Sometimes the therapist gently moves a joint with her hands. **Massage**, heat or cold can also be part of the treatment. It is important to do the exercises **at home** as well. Only those who practise regularly get fit again quickly.

**Basic insurance** pays for physiotherapy if a doctor has **prescribed** it. A prescription is for a certain number of sessions, usually up to nine. If you need more, the doctor issues a new prescription. The **deductible** and **excess** still apply. After an accident, accident insurance often pays for employees.

In Switzerland, physiotherapy is studied at a **university of applied sciences**. The course takes several years and ends with a bachelor’s degree. Physiotherapists work in their own practices, in hospitals, rehabilitation clinics or with sports teams. Many top athletes have their own physiotherapist.

gewusst: The word physiotherapy comes from Greek and roughly means “treatment with natural means”.
Even top athletes often do physiotherapy for months after an injury before they compete again.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who cannot go home at lunchtime because of work has to eat out. This usually costs more than at home. For this, you can claim a deduction for meals away from home in your tax return.
wichtigste: The meals deduction is part of work expenses.
You can claim it if you cannot go home at lunchtime.
There is a flat-rate deduction per working day, limited per year.
If the employer subsidises the food, the deduction is smaller.
The salary statement shows whether there is a canteen or lunch vouchers.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who eats at home has lower costs than in a restaurant. But anyone who **cannot go home** at lunchtime because of work has **extra costs**. These are part of **work expenses** and may be subtracted from income. This also applies to shift work when you have to eat at your workplace.

You do not have to collect every receipt. There is a **flat-rate deduction** per working day, which has an upper limit per year. The exact amounts are set by the Confederation and the cantons, and they can change. The current figures are in the guidance notes for the tax return.

If the employer offers a **subsidised canteen** or gives **lunch vouchers**, the extra costs are smaller. That is why the deduction is lower too, usually only half. The **salary statement** shows this with a cross. That way the tax office knows which deduction applies.

gewusst: Anyone who could easily go home at lunchtime but still eats out may not claim a deduction.

teile.einleitung: Tax avoidance means legally paying as little tax as possible. This is allowed as long as you stick to the law. What is forbidden, on the other hand, is keeping income quiet or inventing deductions.
wichtigste: Saving tax legally is allowed.
You may claim all permitted deductions in full.
Examples are pillar 3a, work-related expenses and donations.
Keeping income quiet is forbidden and is called evasion.
Invented deductions are forbidden too.
The tax office does not accept very artificial arrangements made only to save tax.

abschnitte.text: The law allows many **deductions**. They lower the income on which you pay tax. Examples are payments into **pillar 3a**, **work-related expenses** such as the journey to work, costs of further training and **donations** to charitable organisations. Anyone who declares all permitted deductions in full is acting legally. This is called **tax avoidance** or tax optimisation.

Anyone who does not declare income or wealth is committing **tax evasion**. Anyone who invents deductions, for example by declaring costs that never existed, is also doing something forbidden. Anyone who forges documents for this is even committing **tax fraud**. Remember: using deductions is allowed, keeping things quiet is not.

Companies also try to save tax. Some shift profits to countries with very low taxes. This is often legal, but controversial. That is why many countries have agreed on a **minimum tax** of 15 per cent for large international groups. Switzerland introduced it after a popular vote in 2023.

gewusst: If an arrangement is unusual, intended only to save tax and has no other purpose, it is called tax circumvention, and the tax office can ignore it.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who **donates** money to a charitable organisation can deduct part of it from their taxes. The organisation must be exempt from tax because it is charitable. At federal level there is a minimum and a maximum limit.
wichtigste: A donation is a gift to an organisation, without anything in return.
Donations to tax-exempt charitable organisations are deductible.
You need a donation receipt for this.
At federal level, donations of 100 francs or more per year are deductible.
At most 20 per cent of net income may be deducted.
The cantons have similar rules.

abschnitte.text: A **donation** is money or something else that you give voluntarily, without getting anything for it. Many people in Switzerland donate, for example, to aid organisations, animal protection, the environment or people in need. Such organisations are called **charitable**, because they work for the good of the general public.

In the tax return, you may only deduct donations to organisations that are **exempt** from tax because they are **charitable**. Presents to friends or family do not count. You need a **donation receipt** from the organisation. Many organisations send these out automatically at the beginning of the year.

For **direct federal tax**, donations only count when they add up to at least **100 francs** a year. You may deduct at most **20 per cent of net income**. So anyone who donates a very large amount cannot deduct all of it. The **cantons** have similar rules, but the amounts may differ slightly.

Before making a donation, it makes sense to check whether an organisation is trustworthy. In Switzerland there is the **Zewo seal of approval** for this. It shows that an organisation handles the money carefully and reports openly about it. You can also donate time, for example as a **volunteer** in a club, but that cannot be deducted.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the countries where people donate a lot of money for charitable purposes.
Companies may also deduct donations to charitable organisations from their profits up to a limit.

teile.einleitung: Non-occupational accident insurance, NBU for short, covers accidents in your free time. It is part of compulsory accident insurance for employees in Switzerland. Anyone who works enough hours for the same employer is insured automatically.
wichtigste: The NBU covers accidents outside work, for example during sport or in the home.
It is compulsory for employees who work at least 8 hours a week for the same employer.
Hours with different employers are not added together.
The premium may be deducted from wages and appears on the payslip.
Anyone who does not have NBU needs accident cover through their health insurer.
The rules are set out in the Accident Insurance Act, UVG for short.

abschnitte.text: A **non-occupational accident** does not happen at work but in your free time. It might be a fall while skiing, a bike accident at the weekend or a slip in the kitchen. Accidents at work, on the other hand, are called **occupational accidents**. For employees, there is separate insurance for both under the **UVG**. The employer pays for occupational accident insurance.

Anyone who works at least **8 hours a week** for the same employer is insured under the NBU. If someone works 6 hours each at two companies, this is not added together. Then they are not insured against accidents in their free time at either of the two companies. With fewer than 8 hours, accidents on the way to work count as occupational accidents. For other accidents in your free time, you need **accident cover from your health insurer**.

The NBU premium is usually paid by the **employees**. The employer deducts it directly from wages. On the **payslip** it usually appears as the abbreviation NBU. Some employers voluntarily pay all or part of the premium. Occupational accident insurance, on the other hand, is always paid for by the employer.

Accident insurance pays the **treatment costs**, in other words the doctor, hospital and therapy. Unlike with health insurance, there is no deductible and no excess. If you cannot work, you receive a **daily allowance** to replace part of your wages. Anyone who is insured through the NBU can have accident cover excluded from their health insurance and so save on the premium. When the job ends, you have to include it again.

gewusst: For an accident covered by the NBU, there is no deductible and no excess.
Suva is the largest accident insurer in Switzerland and was founded in 1918.

teile.einleitung: The deductible is the amount you first pay yourself every year in basic insurance. Only after that does the health insurer contribute to the costs. Anyone who chooses a higher deductible pays a lower premium.
wichtigste: The **deductible** applies per calendar year and starts again at zero on **1 January**.
Adults choose between **300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 francs**.
For children, the standard deductible is **0 francs**, and up to 600 francs can be chosen.
A higher deductible brings a **lower premium**.
After the deductible you also pay an **excess** of 10 per cent.
You can change the deductible with effect from 1 January.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who goes to the doctor receives a bill. In basic insurance you first pay these bills **yourself** until the deductible is reached. An example: Sara has a deductible of 300 francs. Her first doctor’s bill of the year costs 120 francs. Because that is less than the deductible, Sara pays the whole bill herself. On **1 January** the deductible starts again at zero.

For adults, **300 francs** is the standard deductible. There are also five **optional deductibles**: 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 francs. Altogether that makes six levels. The highest deductible is **2500 francs**. Anyone who chooses it pays the lowest premium, but bears more of the costs themselves if they fall ill.

For children, the standard deductible is **0 francs**. But parents can also choose an optional deductible of 100 to 600 francs for their child, in steps of **100 francs**. This makes the premium for the child a little lower. A deductible of 0 francs only exists for children up to 18.

A high deductible tends to be worth it for people who **rarely go to the doctor**. They save money with the lower premium. Anyone who is often ill or needs medicines regularly quickly pays a lot themselves with a high deductible. For these people a **low deductible** is often cheaper. It is important that you actually have the money for the deductible in an emergency.

You can change the deductible with effect from **1 January** of a new year. Anyone who wants a **lower deductible** must tell the insurer by the end of November. After the deductible comes the **excess**: you pay 10 per cent of the further costs, up to a maximum amount per year. For children, this maximum is half as high as for adults.

gewusst: The German and French word “Franchise” for the deductible comes from French and is connected with “franc”, meaning free.
For some preventive services, for example certain vaccination programmes, you do not have to pay a deductible.

teile.einleitung: In basic insurance you are allowed to change your health insurer. Many people do this to save on premiums, because the services are the same at all insurers.
wichtigste: Every insurer must accept every person into basic insurance.
The services of basic insurance are the same at all insurers.
Before changing, you compare the premiums for the place where you live.
It is best to send the notice of cancellation by registered post.
The old insurance only ends once the new insurer has confirmed that it has accepted you.
Basic and supplementary insurance are separate contracts.

abschnitte.text: In **basic insurance**, the services are set by law and are the same everywhere. But the **premiums** differ depending on the insurer, where you live, the deductible and the model. That is why it is worth comparing premiums, for example with the Confederation’s premium calculator. Changing is only worth it if the new insurer really is cheaper.

In basic insurance, the **obligation to accept** applies. Every insurer must accept you, no matter how old or how healthy you are. It may not ask any health questions. This is different with supplementary insurance: there the insurer may ask questions and can also turn someone down.

First you sign up with the new insurer. Then you cancel with the old insurer in good time, most safely by **registered letter**. That way you can prove that the cancellation arrived. The old insurance only ends once the new insurer has **confirmed** to it that it is insuring the person. This way nobody is left without insurance. Anyone who still has unpaid premiums and is facing debt enforcement can only change once everything has been paid.

abschnitte.titel: Supplementary insurance and a new card
abschnitte.text: **Supplementary insurance** is a separate contract. It stays with the old insurer if you do not cancel it. You should not give it up too hastily, because a new insurer would require a health check. After changing, you show the **insurance card of the new insurer** at the doctor’s and at the pharmacy.

gewusst: Health insurers have to announce their new premiums each autumn so that people can still change in time.
You can have basic insurance with one insurer and supplementary insurance with another.

teile.einleitung: In many Swiss municipalities, schoolchildren regularly go to a **school dental check-up**. A dentist looks to see whether their teeth are healthy. The municipality organises this and often pays part of the cost.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, school dental care is a matter for the cantons and municipalities.
Schoolchildren are usually checked once a year.
The municipality often pays part of the costs.
Specialists show the class how to brush their teeth properly.
Basic health insurance usually does not pay for normal dental treatment.
A healthy diet and brushing your teeth protect against tooth decay.

abschnitte.text: At the **school dental check-up**, a dentist looks into your mouth. They check whether there is any **tooth decay**, meaning holes in the teeth. They also check whether the teeth are growing straight. If something is not right, the parents get a report and can arrange treatment.

In Switzerland, **school dental care** is regulated by the cantons. Many cantons require the **municipalities** to offer a yearly check-up. The municipality works together with dentists for this. It often pays part of the costs with **tax money**. Big cities have their own **school dental clinics**.

Besides the check-up there is **prophylaxis**, meaning prevention. **School dental hygienists** visit classes and show how to brush your teeth properly. The children learn that **sugar** harms their teeth. Toothpaste with **fluoride** makes the tooth enamel stronger. Brushing twice a day is a good rule.

**Basic health insurance** usually does not pay for normal dental treatment. So parents have to pay for it themselves. That is why many municipalities support the check-up for children. In this way problems are discovered early, before they become expensive. Families with little money can often receive extra contributions.

gewusst: Thanks to school dental care and prevention, children in Switzerland today have much less tooth decay than a few decades ago.
Milk teeth fall out, but healthy milk teeth help the permanent teeth to grow in the right place.

teile.einleitung: The bicycle vignette was a small sticker that you used to have to put on your bike every year. It was proof of liability insurance. It was abolished in Switzerland in 2012.
wichtigste: For decades the bicycle vignette was compulsory on bikes.
It proved that there was liability insurance.
It was abolished in 2012.
Today, private liability insurance usually covers damage caused with a bike.
Without insurance, you have to pay for any damage yourself.
