abschnitte.text: The **bicycle vignette** was a coloured sticker with the year on it. You bought a new one every year, for example at the post office or in a bike shop. It came with **liability insurance**. This paid if you caused damage to someone with your bike, for example scratching a car.

Almost all households in Switzerland have **private liability insurance**. This usually also covers damage caused with a bike. So the vignette was mostly a duplicate. That is why parliament decided to abolish it, and since 2012 it has no longer been needed.

Today, the family’s **private liability insurance** usually covers damage that you cause with your bike. Anyone who does not have such insurance has to pay for any damage themselves. That is why it is worth checking whether the family is insured. Fast e-bikes have their own rules with a number plate.

gewusst: Many collectors keep old bicycle vignettes, because every year had a different colour.

teile.einleitung: Visits to the doctor, hospitals and medicines cost a lot of money. These health costs are largely paid for through health insurance premiums. When costs rise, premiums rise too.
wichtigste: Switzerland has one of the **most expensive health systems** in the world.
In 2022, health costs were over **90 billion francs**.
The **premiums** for basic insurance depend on health costs.
The costs are paid by insured people, the cantons and households.
Anyone who uses treatments sensibly helps to keep costs down.
People on a small income receive a **premium reduction**.

abschnitte.titel: What the money is needed for
abschnitte.text: **Health costs** include treatment in doctors’ surgeries and **hospitals**, medicines, care homes, therapies and much more. A large part of the money goes to hospitals and outpatient treatment. The salaries of doctors, nurses and pharmacists are also part of it. Switzerland has a very good, but also very expensive health system.

Health costs in Switzerland have been rising for many years. One reason is that people are living **longer** and need treatment more often in old age. Another reason is **medical progress**: new equipment and medicines help a lot, but are often expensive. The number of treatments is also increasing.

A large part is paid for through basic insurance **premiums**. When costs rise, premiums rise too. The **cantons** pay part of hospital costs with tax money. Insured people also pay themselves through the **deductible** and the **excess**. People who earn little receive a **premium reduction** from the canton.

Everyone can help a little so that costs rise less steeply. Go to the doctor when it is **necessary**, and not to A&E for every little thing. If possible, choose a **generic** instead of an expensive original. **Check bills** and report mistakes to the health insurer. And people who live healthily need treatment less often.

gewusst: Switzerland’s health costs are analysed every year by the Federal Statistical Office.
A single day in hospital can cost more than a thousand francs.

teile.einleitung: Premium arrears arise when someone does not pay their health insurance premiums. The insurer may not cancel basic insurance because of this. But it can claim the money with reminders and debt enforcement proceedings.
wichtigste: If premiums are unpaid, the insurer first sends reminders.
After that it can start debt enforcement proceedings.
Basic insurance may not be cancelled because of debts.
As long as premiums are unpaid, you cannot change insurer.
Anyone who has trouble paying should check early on whether they can get a premium reduction and look for help.

abschnitte.text: If someone does not pay the premium, the insurer first sends a **reminder**. This is a note that money is still owed. If the person still does not pay, the insurer can start **debt enforcement proceedings**. The debt enforcement office helps to claim the money. Fees are then often added to the unpaid premiums.

Basic insurance is **compulsory**. That is why the insurer may **not cancel** it because of debts. So you stay insured even if premiums are unpaid. But as long as the debts have not been paid, you **cannot change insurer**. If debt enforcement is unsuccessful, the **canton** takes over a large part of the unpaid claims.

Anyone who has trouble paying the premiums should not wait. You can apply to the canton for a **premium reduction**. A lower premium through a different deductible or a different model can also help. For money worries, **debt advice services** offer free help. Often you can also agree a payment plan with the insurer.

gewusst: Debt enforcement is entered in the debt enforcement register. This can cause problems later, for example when looking for a flat.

teile.einleitung: Cough syrup is a medicine for coughs. It often tastes sweet, but it is not a drink. You only take as much as the doctor, the pharmacist or the adults say.
wichtigste: **Cough syrup** is a **medicine**, even if it tastes nice.
You only take the **amount** that is stated on the packet or that the adults tell you.
To measure it, you use the **measuring spoon** or measuring cup from the packet.
Too much medicine can **harm** the body.
There are syrups for **dry** coughs and for **chesty** coughs.

abschnitte.text: **Coughing** is a protective reaction of the body. With a powerful burst of air, it clears mucus, dust or germs from the airways. A cough often comes with a **cold**. Usually it goes away by itself after a few days or weeks. Anyone who coughs holds the crook of their elbow in front of their mouth so as not to infect others.

There are different kinds of **cough syrup**. For a **dry, tickly cough**, a syrup that calms the urge to cough helps. For a **chesty cough**, a syrup that loosens the mucus helps, so that you can cough it up more easily. The doctor or the pharmacist knows which one is suitable. There are special syrups for children.

Even if a cough syrup tastes good, it is **not a drink**. You only take as much as it says in the **package leaflet** or as the adults tell you. To measure it, you use the **measuring spoon** or the measuring cup that comes in the packet. An ordinary tablespoon is not accurate enough. Too much medicine can **do harm**.

With a cough it helps to **drink plenty**, for example warm tea. Moist air in the room can soothe the throat. Enough **sleep** helps the body to get well. If the cough lasts a long time, or you have a fever or trouble breathing, go to the doctor. Always keep medicines safely in the **home first aid kit**.

gewusst: A cough can be very fast: the air shoots out of the lungs with great force.
Many cough syrups have a sweet taste so that children find them easier to swallow.

teile.einleitung: **Taking care** means treating things carefully. Benches, play equipment and bins in the park belong to everyone. If they get broken, everyone pays for the repair with their taxes.
wichtigste: Public things such as park benches are paid for with tax money.
If something gets broken, the repair costs everyone's money.
Deliberate damage is called vandalism.
Damage to property is a criminal offence in Switzerland.
In many places, anyone who leaves rubbish lying around can be fined.
Taking care means everyone can enjoy a place for longer.

abschnitte.text: In a **park** there are benches, paths, fountains, play equipment and flower beds. These things do not belong to one single person but to the **municipality**, and so to everyone. They were built with **tax money**. That is why everyone may use them. At the same time, everyone has the task of looking after them well.

If a bench is damaged or play equipment is destroyed, the municipality has to **repair** or replace it. For this it needs workers, materials and time. The money again comes from **taxes**. This money is then missing for other things, for example a new playground. So taking care saves money for everyone.

Anyone who deliberately breaks things or daubs them with paint is committing **vandalism**. In law this is called **damage to property**, and it is a criminal offence. Anyone who is caught has to pay for the damage and can be punished. Leaving rubbish lying around, **littering**, can also cost a **fine** in many cantons and municipalities.

Taking care starts with small things: throwing rubbish in the bin, using play equipment properly and leaving plants alone. Anyone who sees that something is broken can report it to the municipality. Many municipalities have a telephone number or an **app** for this. That way the park stays nice for everyone, including the children who come later.

gewusst: Cleaning up litter costs municipalities in Switzerland a lot of money every year.
In some municipalities, school classes help on the yearly clean-up day.

teile.einleitung: Taxes are money that people and companies pay to the state. They pay for things that are useful to everyone, such as schools, roads and the fire brigade. You do not get a present of your own for your taxes.
wichtigste: Taxes are payments to the municipality, the canton and the Confederation.
They pay for things for everyone, for example schools and roads.
You do not get anything directly in return for taxes.
Private things such as toys or your mid-morning snack are paid for by your family.
There are direct taxes such as income tax.
There are indirect taxes such as VAT.
Taxes have existed for a very long time.

abschnitte.text: With **taxes** the state pays for shared tasks. These include **schools**, **roads**, the **police**, the **fire brigade**, hospitals and much more. Every person can use these things. However, you do not get a present of your own back for taxes. The benefit goes to everyone together.

abschnitte.titel: What do you pay for yourself?
abschnitte.text: Everything that belongs to a person or a family is not paid for with taxes. Your **toys**, your clothes or your **mid-morning snack** (in Switzerland called “Znüni”) are bought by your family or by you. The school where you eat your snack, on the other hand, is paid for with taxes. Remember: what belongs to you, you pay for yourself.

There are **direct taxes**, which you pay directly to the state. Examples are income tax on wages and wealth tax. There are also **indirect taxes**. They are included in the price of goods, for example **VAT**. Even children pay this when they buy something.

There have always been shared tasks. A very long time ago, people already pooled things together, for example for paths, wells or protection. In the Middle Ages, farmers often had to hand over the **tithe**, in other words a tenth of their harvest. Today taxes are paid in francs, and in Switzerland the people often help decide how high they are.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the municipalities, the cantons and the Confederation collect their own taxes, which is rather rare around the world.
Direct federal tax is only allowed for a limited time in the Federal Constitution and has to be extended by the people again and again.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who pays insurance premiums, for example for health insurance, can deduct part of them in their tax return. This is called the insurance deduction. However, it has an upper limit.
wichtigste: Health insurance and accident insurance premiums are part of the insurance deduction.
Interest on savings capital often falls under the same deduction too.
The deduction is only possible up to a maximum amount.
It often covers only part of the premiums paid.
Premium reductions you have received must be taken into account.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, **health insurance** is compulsory for everyone. The **premiums** for it, as well as those for accident insurance or life insurance, can be declared in the tax return. They are part of the **insurance deduction**. Contributions that the employer deducts directly from wages, such as for the AVS, are treated differently.

The insurance deduction is **limited**. Different maximum amounts apply to married people, single people and for each child. Because health insurance premiums have risen in recent years, the deduction often covers only **part** of the premiums. The exact amounts differ depending on the canton and for federal tax.

Families on a small income receive a **premium reduction** from the canton. These contributions must be subtracted from the premiums. You may only deduct what you have really paid yourself. That way nobody gets a double advantage.

gewusst: Payments into pillar 3a are not part of the insurance deduction but have a separate deduction.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, men have a duty to serve. Anyone who does not do military service, civilian service or civil protection service has to pay a replacement charge. It is called the military service exemption tax.
wichtigste: Swiss men have a duty to serve.
Anyone who does not do their service pays the military service exemption tax.
The amount of the charge depends on income.
It is collected by the canton on behalf of the Confederation.
For women, military service is voluntary.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Constitution** says that every Swiss man must do **military service**. Anyone who cannot do so for reasons of conscience does **civilian service** instead. Anyone who is not fit for military service can be assigned to **civil protection**. For women, service is voluntary.

Men liable for service who do not do their service in a given year pay a **replacement charge**. The amount depends on their **income**. Anyone who earns more pays more. It is collected by the **cantons**, but most of the money goes to the **Confederation**.

Not everyone has to pay the charge. Anyone who cannot serve because of a significant **disability**, for example, is exempt under certain conditions. Anyone who catches up on their service later can get part of the charges they paid back. The exact rules are set out in the law on the military service exemption tax.

gewusst: Swiss men who live abroad can also be liable for the charge in certain circumstances.

teile.einleitung: Taxes are money that all people and companies pay to the state so that it can carry out shared tasks. In Switzerland, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities collect taxes. This money pays for schools, roads, hospitals and much more.
wichtigste: The state needs taxes for schools, roads, hospitals and much more.
In Switzerland, the Confederation, the canton and the municipality collect taxes.
VAT is included in the price of many goods and services.
With the tax return you declare your income and wealth every year.
Cantons and municipalities partly set their own taxes.
Pillar 3a is voluntary saving for old age that you can deduct from your taxable income.
From the year in which you turn 18, you are liable for tax yourself.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **federal state** with three levels: the Confederation, 26 cantons and around 2,100 municipalities. All three collect taxes and use them to carry out their tasks. The Confederation pays for things like the army, national roads and universities such as the ETH. Cantons and municipalities mainly finance schools, the police, hospitals and the upkeep of municipal roads.

The best-known federal tax is **VAT**, which is included in the price of almost all goods, and the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent since 2024. There is also direct federal tax on income and profits. Cantons and municipalities collect income and wealth taxes as well as taxes on inheritances and on profits from land. There are also smaller taxes, such as the dog tax or church tax.

Because cantons and municipalities partly set their own taxes, there are big differences. Zug and Schwyz are considered particularly low-tax, while in cantons such as Geneva, Neuchâtel or Bern people often pay more. This competition is called **tax competition**. So that the differences do not become too great, there is **fiscal equalisation** between the cantons.

Anyone who is an adult fills in a **tax return** every year. In it you declare your wages, other income, accounts and wealth. At the same time you may make deductions, for example for the journey to work or payments into pillar 3a. From all this, the tax office calculates the taxes for the Confederation, the canton and the municipality.

In Switzerland the people can vote on many tax questions. At municipal level, voters often decide on the **tax multiplier** at the municipal assembly. At federal level, a higher VAT rate needs the approval of the people and the cantons. This right to have a say is almost unique in the world.

Even children already pay taxes, namely VAT when they go shopping. But they only need their own tax return from the year in which they turn 18. Until then, children’s income and wealth are usually taxed through their parents. An apprentice’s wage, however, is taxed for the child themselves even before then.

begriffe.erklaerung: Compulsory payments to the state that pay for shared tasks.
Number with which the municipality or canton sets the level of the tax.
Tax that is included in the price of many goods and services.
Voluntary saving for old age with a tax advantage.
Cantons and municipalities try to attract residents and companies with low taxes.

gewusst: Depending on where they live, a family with the same income in Switzerland can pay several thousand francs more or less in tax.
In many municipalities, residents vote on the tax multiplier every year at the municipal assembly.
VAT is the Confederation’s largest source of income.

teile.einleitung: People who work sometimes have expenses for their job, for example for tools or specialist books. In the tax return you may claim the deduction for **other work-related expenses** for this. It lowers your taxable income.
wichtigste: Other work-related expenses are smaller expenses that you have for your job.
Examples are work clothes, tools, specialist literature and a study at home.
There is usually a flat rate for this as a percentage of net wages.
For the Confederation, the flat rate is 3 per cent of net wages, with a minimum and maximum amount.
Anyone with higher costs can claim them with receipts.
The journey to work and meals are separate deductions and are not included.

abschnitte.text: **Other work-related expenses** include expenses that you have because of your work. These are, for example, **work clothes**, **tools**, **specialist books** or a computer that you need for work. A **study** at home can also be included if you work there regularly. Costs for hobbies or private things do not count.

So that not everyone has to collect every small receipt, there is a **flat rate**. It is calculated as a **percentage of net wages**. For direct federal tax it is 3 per cent, with a **minimum amount** and a **maximum amount**. The cantons have their own rules, which look similar. You get the flat rate without having to prove anything.

Anyone who spends more than the flat rate can deduct the **actual costs**. For this you need **receipts**, for example till receipts. The tax office can ask for them and check them. It is important that the expenses were really necessary for the job and were not paid for by the employer.

Other work-related expenses are only one part of **work expenses**. There are also separate deductions for the **journey to work**, in other words a ticket, a bike or a car. There is also a deduction for **meals** eaten out when you cannot eat at home. There is a separate deduction for **further training** too.

gewusst: In many of the cantons’ online tax programs, the flat rate for other work-related expenses is filled in automatically.
Apprentices may also deduct work expenses if they earn a wage.

teile.einleitung: The notice period sets the date by which you have to cancel with your health insurer so that the change works. Anyone who misses the deadline stays with the old insurer for another year.
wichtigste: To change on 1 January, the cancellation must arrive by the end of November.
If it arrives too late, you stay insured as before for another year.
What matters is when it arrives at the insurer.
With a 300-franc deductible and the standard model, there is also a deadline for the end of June.
Anyone who cancels early is on the safe side.

abschnitte.text: A **deadline** is a period of time within which you have to do something. In basic insurance, the notice period for changing at the end of the year is **one month**. So the cancellation must reach the insurer by **30 November**. Then you are insured with the new insurer from 1 January.

Paul only sends his cancellation on **15 December**. That is too late. The insurer does not have to accept the cancellation, and Paul stays with the old insurer for **another year**. So he pays the previous premium for another year, even if another insurer would be cheaper. He can only cancel again next autumn.

Insurers announce their new premiums in autumn. After that you have a few weeks to compare and cancel. Anyone who sends the cancellation **early** and by **registered post** does not need to worry. With the **standard deductible** and the **standard model**, you can also change with three months’ notice at the **end of June**.

gewusst: Some insurers also accept a cancellation by email, but a registered letter is the easiest to prove.
Different, longer notice periods often apply to supplementary insurance.

teile.einleitung: The state is the community of all the people in a country with shared rules and authorities. In Switzerland, the state is made up of three levels: municipality, canton and Confederation. All three receive taxes.
wichtigste: Switzerland has three levels of state: municipality, canton and Confederation.
All three levels collect taxes.
With tax money, the state carries out tasks for everyone.
Switzerland is a federal state with 26 cantons.
Power is divided between parliament, government and the courts.
In Switzerland, the people can often have a direct say.

abschnitte.text: A **state** has a territory, a people and a state authority that makes and enforces rules. The most important rules of Switzerland are written in the **Federal Constitution**. The state provides things such as security, schools and roads. For this it needs money, and a large part of this money comes from taxes.

In Switzerland there is the **municipality**, the **canton** and the **Confederation**. Each level has its own tasks. The municipality looks after things like primary school and rubbish collection. The canton is responsible for the police and hospitals, for example. The Confederation looks after the army and the AVS, among other things. All three receive taxes.

Power in the state is divided, and this is called the **separation of powers**. Parliament makes the laws. The government carries them out. The courts make judgements when there is a dispute. At federal level these are the Federal Assembly, the Federal Council and the Federal Supreme Court. This way, no single body can decide everything on its own.

Switzerland is a **direct democracy**. Voters not only elect their representatives, they also vote on specific issues. With an **initiative** they can propose changes. With a **referendum** they can vote on a law. Taxes are also often decided at the ballot box.

gewusst: The Federal Council has seven members who together form the government.
In the Federal Palace in Bern, the National Council with 200 members and the Council of States with 46 members hold their sessions.

teile.einleitung: After the tax return, the tax office works out how much someone has to pay. Then it sends a tax bill. Income tax goes to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality.
wichtigste: The tax bill comes from the tax office.
It shows how much tax you have to pay.
It is based on the tax return.
Income tax goes to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality.
Usually everything comes through the cantonal tax office.
Often there is first a provisional bill and then a final one.

abschnitte.text: Adults fill in a **tax return** every year. The tax office checks it and uses it to calculate the taxes. This decision is called the **tax assessment**. Afterwards you receive a **tax bill**. Anyone who disagrees with the assessment can lodge an **objection** within a deadline.

Mia lives in Lucerne. Her **income tax** goes to all three levels: **direct federal tax** to the Confederation, **cantonal tax** to the canton and **municipal tax** to her municipality. But she does not have to pay three offices separately. Usually everything comes through the cantonal tax office, which then distributes the money.

Many cantons send a **provisional bill** during the year. It is an estimate, often based on the previous year. Later the **final bill** follows. If you have paid too much, you get money back. If you have paid too little, you have to transfer the rest. You can often pay in instalments too.

The bill states the date by which it must be paid. Anyone who pays late has to pay **default interest**. Anyone who does not pay at all receives reminders and, in the worst case, **debt enforcement proceedings**. If you really cannot pay, you should contact the tax office early.

gewusst: In many cantons, anyone who pays their taxes early is credited with a little interest.

teile.einleitung: For children, parents pay a separate, lower premium to the health insurer. The law aims to ease the burden on families, because children still get all the services of basic insurance.
wichtigste: The children’s premium applies up to 18.
The law provides for lower premiums for children.
Children receive the same services as adults.
For children there is no minimum deductible, and it can also be 0 francs.
For children, the excess is limited to 350 francs a year.
The cantons reduce children’s premiums for families on low and middle incomes.

abschnitte.text: Families with children have a lot of expenses. That is why the **Health Insurance Act** requires premiums for children to be lower than for adults. This is a form of **solidarity**: adults without children bear a larger share of the costs. Even so, children are insured just as well.

Separate rules apply to children. For children the **deductible** can be 0 francs, but you can also choose a higher one of up to 600 francs. The **excess** is 10 % of the costs, but at most 350 francs a year. For adults, this limit is twice as high.

The cantons pay **premium reductions** to households on a small income. For children from families on low and middle incomes, they have to reduce the premium especially strongly. How much a family gets depends on the canton and on the income. Some insurers also give a discount from the second or third child.

The children’s premium applies until the end of the year in which a child turns 18. After that comes the premium for **young adults** from 19 to 25. It is higher, but usually still lower than the premium for adults from 26.

gewusst: The premium for a child differs depending on where you live, because insurers set their premiums by canton and region.
Even a baby must have its own basic insurance.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, every person who lives here must have basic insurance with a health insurer. This has been governed by the Health Insurance Act, KVG for short, since 1996. You can choose your health insurer freely, and every insurer must accept everyone.
wichtigste: Basic insurance is compulsory for all people who live in Switzerland.
A health insurer may not turn anyone down for basic insurance, it must accept everyone.
The services of basic insurance are the same at all health insurers.
Premiums are graded by age, and from 26 you pay the full adult premium.
Anyone who wants to change at the start of the year usually has to cancel by the end of November.
As a rule, basic insurance does not pay for normal dental treatment such as check-ups or fillings.
Supplementary insurance is voluntary, and the health insurer may turn down an application.

abschnitte.text: The **Health Insurance Act (KVG)** was approved by the people in 1994 and came into force on 1 January 1996. It made **basic insurance** compulsory for everyone. Anyone who moves to Switzerland or is born here must be insured within three months. It is best to register babies before they are born. The cantons check that everyone really is insured.

Basic insurance covers treatment for illness, maternity and accidents, if you are not insured against accidents elsewhere. This includes visits to the doctor, hospital stays in the general ward and medicines on the **list of specialities**. Certain check-ups and vaccinations are also included. As a rule, it does not pay for normal **dental treatment** such as check-ups or fillings. For this you need supplementary insurance, or you pay yourself.

Every month you pay a **premium**. In 2026, the average premium for adults was just under 400 francs a month. Children up to 18 pay much less, and young adults from 19 to 25 a little less. From 26 you pay the full adult premium. In addition, you bear part of the costs yourself through the **deductible** and the excess.

Every autumn, health insurers announce their premiums for the next year. Anyone who wants to change usually has to have submitted their cancellation to the health insurer by the **end of November**. Then the new insurer applies from 1 January. On the Confederation’s website priminfo.admin.ch you can compare premiums. Because the services are the same, changing can often save money without losing anything.

As well as basic insurance, there is voluntary **supplementary insurance**. It pays, for example, for braces, glasses or a room in the semi-private ward. Here the health insurer may turn down an application or make reservations. That is why it is worth taking out supplementary insurance while you are young and healthy. You do not have to have basic and supplementary insurance with the same insurer.

begriffe.erklaerung: Health Insurance Act, which governs health insurance in Switzerland.
Compulsory insurance with the same services at all health insurers.
Voluntary insurance for extras such as braces or a single room.
Monthly amount that you pay to the health insurer.

gewusst: Anyone who does not take out insurance themselves is assigned to a health insurer by the canton.
Since the KVG was introduced in 1996, average premiums have more than doubled.
The official name of basic insurance is “compulsory health care insurance”, OKP for short.

teile.einleitung: The polluter pays principle is a simple rule: whoever causes costs should also pay for them. In Switzerland it applies especially to fees and to environmental protection. Examples are the rubbish bag fee and the water charge.
wichtigste: Whoever uses a service or causes costs pays for it.
You pay taxes for everything shared, and fees for a specific service.
The rubbish bag fee is a well-known example.
Water and waste water are also often paid for according to how much is used.
The principle is set out in the Environmental Protection Act and in the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: In many municipalities you buy special **rubbish bags** or fee stickers. Anyone who produces a lot of rubbish needs more bags and pays more. Anyone who separates and recycles saves money. This is the **polluter pays principle** in everyday life.

You pay **taxes** without receiving a specific service in return. With them the state pays for schools, roads or the police for everyone. **Fees**, on the other hand, are paid for a specific service, for example for **water** or a passport. For water, the fee often depends on **consumption**.

The polluter pays principle is laid down in the **Environmental Protection Act** and in the **Federal Constitution**. Whoever puts a strain on the environment should bear the costs. This is meant to encourage people and companies to be more economical. The result is less rubbish and less pollution.

gewusst: The advance recycling fee that you pay when you buy electrical appliances follows a similar idea.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, you can reach the police on the number 117. The police help when people are in danger, in accidents or when something illegal is happening. The call is free.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, you can reach the police on 117.
The ambulance service has 144 and the fire brigade 118.
A call to 117 is free.
In Switzerland there are mainly cantonal police forces, and many cities have their own city police.
The police maintain safety and order.

abschnitte.text: You call **117** when people are in danger or something illegal is happening. That might be a **burglary**, a theft or a violent argument. The police also often come to a **road accident**. If someone is injured, you also call 144. The police can also alert the other rescue services themselves.

In Switzerland, the police are mainly a matter for the **cantons**. Every canton has a **cantonal police force**. Many larger cities also have their own **city police**. At federal level there is the Federal Office of Police, **fedpol** for short. It deals with special tasks, for example working together with other countries.

The police maintain **safety and order**. They direct traffic, check speeds and help at accidents. They find out who has done something illegal. Police officers also visit schools and explain how to stay safe in traffic. You may turn to them at any time if you need help.

gewusst: You can call 117 free of charge from any phone throughout Switzerland.
In Switzerland, policing is the task of the cantons, which is why uniforms and cars look slightly different depending on the canton.

teile.einleitung: A medicine that a doctor prescribes is meant for one particular person. You must not simply pass it on or take other people’s medicines.
wichtigste: A prescribed medicine is only intended for one person.
The doctor chooses the remedy and the amount to suit age, weight and illness.
For another child it may be wrong or dangerous.
With medicines, always ask your parents, the doctor or the pharmacy.
The package leaflet explains how to take the medicine correctly.

abschnitte.text: When a doctor prescribes a **medicine**, she thinks carefully: what illness does the person have? How old and how heavy are they? Can they tolerate the remedy? Then she decides the **dose**, in other words how much to take and how often. That is why such a medicine is only intended for this one person.

Mia has a cough, and her brother still has tablets from the doctor. Even so, she must not simply take them. Her cough may have a completely different cause. The amount may be too large or too small for her. Some remedies can have **side effects** or even be **dangerous** if taken wrongly.

For many medicines you need a **prescription** from the doctor. Every packet contains a **package leaflet**. It says what the remedy is for, how to take it and what side effects it can have. In Switzerland, the authority **Swissmedic** checks whether a medicine is safe before it may be sold.

If you are unsure, ask your parents, the doctor or at the **pharmacy**. Pharmacists are experts on medicines and are happy to give advice. Old medicines are taken back to the pharmacy instead of being kept or thrown in the bin.

gewusst: In Switzerland, if someone is poisoned by medicines, Tox Info Suisse helps on the number 145.
Many medicines for children come as a syrup or drops, because they are easier to swallow and easier to dose accurately.

teile.einleitung: Generic medicines are copies of medicines. They contain the same active ingredient as the original but cost less. Anyone who chooses a generic saves their own money and helps to keep health costs down.
wichtigste: A **generic** contains the same **active ingredient** as the original medicine.
Generics may only be sold once the **patent protection** of the original has expired.
Generics are usually much **cheaper**.
Anyone who chooses the more expensive original without a medical reason pays a **higher excess**.
Doctors and pharmacists advise on whether a generic is suitable.

abschnitte.text: When a company develops a new medicine, it is protected by a **patent**. During this time, only this company may sell the medicine. When the patent protection expires, other companies may also make medicines with the same **active ingredient**. These copies are called **generics**. They must work just as well as the original.

Developing a new medicine takes many years and costs a lot of money. Anyone who makes a generic does not have to do this research again. That is why they can sell the medicine more **cheaply**. Generics often have a different shape, colour or packaging, but the active ingredient is the same. Before a generic may be sold in Switzerland, the authority **Swissmedic** checks it.

Normally, in basic insurance you pay an excess of 10 per cent after the deductible. But if there is a cheaper generic and you still choose the expensive **original**, the insurer charges an **increased excess**. This does not apply if the original is necessary for medical reasons. The doctor has to state this reason on the prescription.

gewusst: The word generic comes from the Latin “genus” and roughly means kind or type.
Generics help to make health costs, and therefore premiums, rise less steeply.

teile.einleitung: Each canton has its own tax law. So that the rules are still similar, there is the Confederation’s Tax Harmonisation Act. It sets shared basic rules, but the cantons decide the tax rates themselves.
wichtigste: To harmonise means to bring into line with one another.
The Tax Harmonisation Act applies to the taxes of the cantons and municipalities.
It covers things like tax liability, the definition of income and procedures.
The cantons still set the tax scales and tax multipliers themselves.
It is the rules that are harmonised, not the level of taxes.

abschnitte.text: In the past, each canton had completely its own rules. What counted as income, which deductions were allowed and how the procedure worked were very different. This was complicated for people and companies that move or work in several cantons. That is why the **Federal Constitution** requires **tax harmonisation**.

The **Tax Harmonisation Act**, StHG for short, was passed in 1990. It sets out who is **liable for tax**, what counts as **income** and **wealth**, and which deductions exist in principle. The **procedure** and the penalties are also regulated in a similar way. The cantons had to adapt their laws to it.

The cantons still decide for themselves **how high** taxes are. They set the **tax scales**, the **tax multipliers** and the amount of many deductions. That is why there are still big differences between the cantons. This is called **formal harmonisation**: the form is the same, the amount is not.

gewusst: The Tax Harmonisation Act came into force in 1993, and the cantons then had several years to adapt.

teile.einleitung: First aid is the help you give immediately after an accident or a sudden illness until experts arrive. Anyone can give first aid. For children it mainly means: quickly fetching an adult.
wichtigste: **First aid** is help until experts arrive.
Fetching help is also helping.
Important emergency numbers in Switzerland: **144** ambulance, **117** police, **118** fire brigade.
The European emergency number **112** also works in Switzerland.
To get a driving licence you have to attend a **first aid course**.
First you make sure that you do not put yourself in danger.

abschnitte.text: First aid means: you help straight away as well as you can. That might be putting a plaster on a small wound. With bigger accidents, the point is to **fetch help** and stay with the injured person. You do not have to be a doctor to give first aid. The important thing is not to look away.

In an accident, a simple sequence applies. First **look**: what has happened? Are there dangers, for example cars? Then **think**: do I need help? And then **act**: call for help and look after the injured person. You never put yourself in danger while doing this.

If a child falls in the playground and cries a lot, it is best to fetch an **adult** straight away, for example the teacher. You can stay with the child, talk to them and comfort them. In an emergency, children may also call **144**. Then you say calmly who you are, where you are and what has happened.

In Switzerland there are several **emergency numbers**: 144 for the ambulance, 117 for the police and 118 for the fire brigade. In case of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** can help on 145. The number **112** applies throughout Europe. Emergency calls are free and also work from a mobile phone.

In Switzerland, anyone who wants to get a **driving licence** first has to attend a **first aid course**. There you learn, for example, how to lay an unconscious person down correctly. Courses are offered by the **Samaritan associations**, among others. There are also special courses for children.

gewusst: The Red Cross was co-founded by Henry Dunant from Geneva. For this he received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
Many public places have a defibrillator, a device that can help when someone’s heart stops. It explains with a voice what you have to do.

teile.einleitung: 112 is the European emergency number. It works in all countries of the European Union and also in Switzerland. This means that anyone travelling abroad only has to remember one single number.
wichtigste: 112 is the shared emergency number in Europe.
It works in all EU countries and also in Switzerland.
The call is free.
In Switzerland, a call to 112 goes to the police, who will help further.
For the ambulance service in Switzerland, however, 144 is the most direct route.

abschnitte.text: In the past, every country in Europe had its own emergency numbers. This was difficult for travellers. That is why **112** was introduced as a shared **European emergency number**. Today it works in all countries of the **European Union**. You can also dial it in Switzerland and in many other countries.

In Switzerland, a call to **112** goes to the **police**. They send help or put you through. There are also the well-known numbers here: **144** for the ambulance service, **117** for the police and **118** for the fire brigade. Anyone who needs an ambulance in Switzerland is best off dialling 144 directly. But anyone who only knows 112 will get help too.

A call to 112 is **free**. You do not need any credit on your mobile phone. On most mobile phones you can even dial the number when the screen is locked. On the phone, as with every emergency call, you say **who**, **where** and **what** has happened.

gewusst: 11 February is European 112 Day, to match the numbers 1 1 2.

teile.einleitung: Basic insurance is the health insurance that is compulsory for everyone in Switzerland. It pays for treatment in case of illness and, for people who are not insured in another way, also in case of accident. The services are the same at all health insurers, but the premiums are not.
wichtigste: **Basic insurance** is **compulsory** for all people who live in Switzerland.
Since 1996 it has been governed by the **Health Insurance Act** (KVG).
Anyone who moves to Switzerland must take out insurance within **3 months**.
The **services** are the same at all health insurers.
Every insurer must accept everyone: the **obligation to accept** applies.
Insurers may **not make a profit** from basic insurance.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland every person must have **basic insurance**, from babies to grandmothers. This is set out in the **Health Insurance Act**, which came into force in 1996. Anyone who moves to Switzerland must take out insurance within **3 months**. The insurance then applies backdated to the date of arrival. For newborn babies, the parents take out the insurance.

The law sets out what basic insurance pays for: for example visits to the doctor, hospital stays in the general ward, many **medicines** and certain check-ups. That is why the **services** are the same at every health insurer. Only the **premiums** and the service differ. The premiums also depend on the canton you live in and on your age.

In basic insurance, the **obligation to accept** applies. Every insurer must accept everyone, no matter how old or how healthy they are. That is why there are **no health questions** and no refusals. This is a big difference from supplementary insurance. There, the insurer may decide for itself whom it accepts.

Health insurers may **not make a profit** from basic insurance. The money from premiums must be used for services and administration. Insurers may only make a profit with **supplementary insurance**. Anyone who is not happy with their insurer can change their basic insurance at the end of the year. The notice must reach the insurer by the end of November.

gewusst: Before 1996, health insurance was voluntary in many cantons.
Because the services are the same everywhere, it is worth comparing premiums between insurers.

teile.einleitung: Washing your hands is one of the simplest and most effective ways of staying healthy. With water and soap you remove dirt and many germs that you cannot see with the naked eye.
wichtigste: There are many germs on your hands that you cannot see.
You should always wash your hands before eating and after going to the toilet.
Washing thoroughly takes about 20 to 30 seconds.
Soap dissolves grease and dirt that germs stick to.
Handwashing protects against colds, flu and stomach bugs.
Finally, you dry your hands well.

abschnitte.text: Every day we touch door handles, banisters, mobile phones and toys. **Germs** stick to our hands as we do so, in other words tiny bacteria and viruses. Many are harmless, but some make you ill. If we then touch our mouth, nose or eyes, they can get into the body. That is why handwashing is an important protection.

It is especially important **before eating** and **after going to the toilet**. It is also worth doing after blowing your nose, coughing or sneezing, after playing outside and after stroking animals. Anyone who cooks washes their hands first. And when you come home, it is best to wash them straight away too.

First you wet your hands and take some **soap**. Then you rub everything well: palms, backs of the hands, between the fingers, the thumbs and the fingertips. This takes about **20 to 30 seconds**, as long as singing “Happy Birthday” twice. Then you rinse off the soap and dry your hands with a clean towel.

Anyone who washes their hands protects not only themselves but also others. That is why good hygiene is especially important in hospitals and doctors’ surgeries. There, people often also use **disinfectant**, which kills germs. Fewer infections also mean fewer visits to the doctor and therefore lower health costs.

gewusst: In the 19th century, the doctor Ignaz Semmelweis in Vienna noticed that far fewer patients fell ill when the doctors disinfected their hands first.
Global Handwashing Day is on 15 October every year.

teile.einleitung: The tax return is a form in which you declare your income and your wealth every year. From this information, the tax office calculates how much tax you have to pay. In Switzerland, you usually fill it in for the first time from the year in which you come of age.
wichtigste: With the tax return you declare your income and wealth every year.
Your first own tax return usually comes from the year in which you turn 18.
In many cantons it has to be submitted by the end of March.
You can fill it in on paper or with software on the computer.
Important documents are the salary statement and the bank statements.
The tax office checks the information and then sends out the assessment.
Anyone who gives false information risks heavy fines.

abschnitte.text: The **tax return** is a kind of report on your own finances. It states how much you earned in the past year and how much wealth you had on 31 December. In Switzerland the principle of **self-declaration** applies, which means you give this information yourself. The tax office trusts it at first, but it also carries out checks.

In Switzerland you usually become liable for tax from the year in which you turn 18. You then receive your first own tax return the following spring. Until then, children are taxed through their parents, and their wealth counts towards the parents’ tax return. Apprentices and students also have to fill in a tax return, even if they earn little.

The **salary statement**, which the employer issues every year, is important. Added to this is information on bank accounts, securities, debts and any car or house. In the section on **deductions** you state what you may subtract from your income, such as travel costs or payments into pillar 3a. All receipts must be enclosed or uploaded.

abschnitte.titel: How do you fill it in?
abschnitte.text: Most cantons offer a free **tax program**, often directly on the internet. The program calculates many things automatically and shows what is still missing. In many cantons the deadline is 31 March, but you can apply for an extension. Anyone who does not submit at all receives a reminder and in the end an estimate from the tax office.

The tax office checks the information and calculates the taxes, and this is called the **tax assessment**. Then you receive a tax bill for the canton, the municipality and the Confederation. Many cantons send provisional bills during the year, which you can pay in instalments. If you disagree with the assessment, you can lodge an objection within 30 days.

begriffe.erklaerung: You declare your income and wealth honestly yourself.
Confirmation from the employer of how much wages you received during the year.
Calculation of the taxes by the tax office.
Latest date by which you have to do something.

gewusst: Anyone who has evaded tax and reports themselves beforehand can avoid a fine once in their lifetime.
Wealth is always counted on the reference date of 31 December, even if you spend it on 2 January.
In Switzerland, married couples fill in a single tax return together.

teile.einleitung: The state often charges special taxes on alcoholic drinks. In Switzerland there are such taxes on beer and on spirits such as schnapps. Wine, on the other hand, is exempt from a special alcohol tax.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there is no special consumption tax on wine.
Beer is taxed with the beer tax.
Spirits such as schnapps are taxed particularly heavily.
VAT still applies to wine too.
Alcohol is forbidden for children and young people and is harmful to health.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, **wine** is grown in many places, especially in Valais, Vaud, Geneva, Ticino and German-speaking Switzerland. After the harvest, called the **grape harvest**, wine is made from the **grapes**. Many families make a living from winegrowing. The vineyards also shape the landscape.

For **beer** there is the **beer tax**, and for **spirits** such as schnapps a separate tax under the Alcohol Act. There is no such special consumption tax on **wine**. Even so, you pay **VAT** when you buy wine, as with almost all goods. On imports, customs duties are added as well.

Alcohol is an **addictive substance** and is particularly harmful to the bodies of young people. That is why there are rules to **protect young people**: beer and wine may only be sold from the age of 16, and spirits only from 18. The taxes on strong alcohol are also meant to help people drink less of it.

gewusst: Most of the revenue from the tax on spirits goes to the AVS and the disability insurance, and part to the cantons for preventing addiction.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, you can reach the fire brigade on the number 118. It comes when there is a fire, but also in many other emergencies. The call is free.
wichtigste: If there is a fire, you dial 118.
For an ambulance, you dial 144.
Most fire brigades in Switzerland are volunteer fire brigades.
In large cities there are also professional fire brigades.
The fire brigade also helps with floods, accidents or spilt oil.
In a fire, you first get yourself to safety.

abschnitte.text: If there is a fire, call **118** straight away. First get yourself and others to safety. Leave the building and never use the **lift**. Close doors behind you so that fire and smoke do not spread so quickly. The **smoke** is often more dangerous than the fire itself.

Most fire brigades in Switzerland are **volunteer fire brigades**. This means that the women and men have normal jobs and turn out when they are alerted. They train regularly. In large cities there are also **professional fire brigades**, which are always ready. In many municipalities there is a **duty to serve in the fire brigade**: anyone who does not take part pays a replacement charge.

The fire brigade does not only help with fires. In **floods** it pumps water out of cellars. In road accidents it frees people trapped in cars. It soaks up spilt **oil** and helps with storm damage. Sometimes it also rescues animals from a difficult situation.

Many fires can be prevented. Never leave **candles** burning unattended. Never put out burning oil in a pan with water, but cover it with a lid or a **fire blanket**. A **smoke alarm** gives an early warning if there is a fire. That leaves more time to get out of the building.

gewusst: Water on burning oil turns to steam instantly and can cause a huge burst of flame.
In Switzerland, most firefighters serve alongside their normal job.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, the cantons and municipalities largely set their own taxes. This puts them in competition: with low taxes they try to attract companies and residents. This has advantages, but also disadvantages.
wichtigste: The cantons largely decide their own taxes.
This creates tax competition.
Low taxes can attract companies and residents.
The canton of Zug has been known for low taxes for decades.
But low taxes also mean less income per person.
VAT is the same in all cantons.

abschnitte.text: The 26 cantons have their own **tax laws**, tax scales and tax multipliers. That is why the tax burden varies a lot from place to place. Cantons with low taxes are attractive for companies and for people who earn well. In this way the cantons **compete** with one another, rather like shops with their prices. This is called **tax competition**.

The canton of **Zug** has had comparatively low taxes for decades. That is why many companies have their headquarters there, including large international groups. Other cantons in Central Switzerland such as Schwyz or Nidwalden are also known for low taxes. In cities and in French-speaking Switzerland, taxes are often higher.

Supporters say that competition forces the cantons to be careful with money. Critics say it leads to a race to the bottom and to less money for important tasks. Low taxes bring **less income** per person, and the canton has to manage its finances well. In addition, housing can become more expensive where many people want to move to.

So that the differences do not become too great, there is **fiscal equalisation**. Financially strong cantons and the Confederation give money to financially weaker cantons. Not all taxes differ: **VAT** is a federal tax and is the same everywhere in Switzerland. Cantonal, municipal and dog taxes, on the other hand, vary from place to place.

gewusst: Direct federal tax is also the same throughout Switzerland, no matter which canton you live in.
Today’s fiscal equalisation between the Confederation and the cantons has applied since 2008.

teile.einleitung: After you have submitted your tax return, the tax office checks the information. Then it calculates how much tax you owe. This process is called tax assessment.
wichtigste: First you submit your tax return, and this is called declaring.
The tax office checks the information and calculates the tax.
The result is set out in the assessment notice.
It shows the taxable income, the wealth and the tax.
If you disagree, you can lodge an objection.

abschnitte.text: Every year you fill in your **tax return** and state your income, wealth and deductions. This is called **declaring**. Then the **tax office** checks the information. It can ask for receipts or ask questions. At the end it decides which amounts apply, and this is the **tax assessment**.

You receive the result in writing in the **assessment notice**. It shows the **taxable income**, the **taxable wealth** and the tax owed. If the tax office has valued something differently from the tax return, this is noted. Then the final tax bill follows.

Anyone who thinks the assessment is wrong can lodge an **objection**. There is a deadline for this, and for direct federal tax it is 30 days. You have to give reasons for the objection. The tax office then checks the case once more.

gewusst: Because checking takes time, during the year you often first pay provisional instalments and only later the final bill.

teile.einleitung: On holiday you want to relax. Even so, you can fall ill or have an accident there too. It is good to know beforehand which insurance helps abroad and what you should take with you.
wichtigste: **Basic insurance** only pays for emergencies abroad up to a limit.
It covers at most **twice** what the treatment would cost in Switzerland.
In the EU and EFTA, the **European Health Insurance Card** helps.
For travel far away, people often take out **travel or supplementary insurance**.
A small **travel first aid kit** belongs in your luggage.

abschnitte.text: If you fall ill in a country of the EU or EFTA, for example in Italy, the **European Health Insurance Card** helps. It is printed on the back of the insurance card. With it you receive the treatment you need, just like the local people. You show the card at the doctor’s or in hospital.

In an **emergency** abroad, basic insurance pays at most twice what the treatment would have cost in Switzerland. In countries with very high medical costs, for example in the **USA**, this is often not enough. That is why many families take out **travel or supplementary insurance**. It can also pay for transport back to Switzerland.

A **travel first aid kit** should contain, for example, plasters, a disinfectant, something for fever and pain, and **sun cream**. Anyone who needs medicines regularly takes enough of them along. For some countries, certain **vaccinations** are recommended before the journey. Ask your family doctor about this in good time.

Many complaints on holiday can be avoided. Protect yourself from the **sun** with a hat, sunglasses and sun cream. In the heat, drink plenty of water. In some countries it is better not to drink tap water. And make a note of the **emergency number** of the country you are visiting; in Europe it is 112.

gewusst: The European emergency number 112 works in all EU countries, but also in Switzerland.
For some destinations you need a vaccination several weeks before you leave.

teile.einleitung: Roads connect villages, towns and countries. They belong to everyone and are therefore paid for together. The municipality, the canton and the Confederation finance them with taxes and other charges.
wichtigste: Most roads are built and repaired with taxes and charges.
There are municipal roads, cantonal roads and national roads.
The Confederation is responsible for the national roads, in other words the motorways.
Part of the money comes from charges on petrol and diesel.
Anyone who drives on the motorway needs a vignette.
Roads have to be maintained regularly.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are **municipal roads**, for example in your neighbourhood. Then there are **cantonal roads**, which connect places with each other. And there are **national roads**, which are mainly the **motorways**. Depending on the kind, the municipality, the canton or the Confederation is responsible for building and maintaining them.

Roads belong to everyone, so we pay for them together. The money comes from **taxes** and other **charges**. An important part comes from the **mineral oil tax** on petrol and diesel. Anyone who wants to drive on the motorway has to buy a **vignette**. This money also goes into the roads.

Roads wear out. There are **potholes**, cracks and damage caused by frost. That is why they have to be repaired regularly. In winter, municipalities and cantons clear the **snow** and spread salt. Bridges, tunnels, cycle paths and pavements are also part of the road network and cost money.

In Switzerland, many roads lead over **passes** and through **tunnels**. Building in the mountains is especially difficult and expensive. A well-known example is the **Gotthard Road Tunnel**, which opened in 1980. Nobody could pay for such large structures alone.

gewusst: Since 2018 there has been a separate federal fund for national roads and transport in urban areas.
The Gotthard Road Tunnel is around 17 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: A municipal **swimming pool** is a place for bathing, swimming and playing. Entry often costs only a little. That is because the municipality pays a large part of the costs with taxes.
wichtigste: There are outdoor pools for the summer and indoor pools for the whole year.
A swimming pool costs a lot of money for water, energy, staff and maintenance.
Entrance fees usually cover only part of the costs.
The municipality pays the rest with tax money.
Many school classes learn to swim at the municipal pool.
Lifeguards make sure everyone is safe.

abschnitte.text: In summer the **outdoor pools** are open, with big pools, slides and lawns to lie on. An **indoor pool** is covered and open all year round. Some municipalities have both; others share a pool with neighbouring municipalities. In Switzerland there are also many **lake baths** and **river baths**.

A swimming pool needs a lot of **water**, which has to be kept clean and is often heated. On top of that come costs for **energy**, **staff** and repairs. Entrance fees are usually not enough to pay for everything. The **municipality** covers the rest with **tax money**. That is why entry is often very cheap for children.

Swimming is important, especially in a country with many lakes and rivers. That is why many **school classes** go to the municipal pool regularly. There the children learn to swim and to move safely in the water. The **SLRG**, the Swiss Lifesaving Society, has developed the **Water Safety Check** for this.

At the pool, **lifeguards** keep watch. Even so, the **swimming rules** are important: never leave children unsupervised near the water, do not swim on a full or empty stomach and do not jump into unfamiliar water. If you keep to the rules, you can enjoy your day at the pool safely.

gewusst: The voters often vote on a new building or an expensive renovation of a municipal pool.
In many Swiss cities you can swim in the river right through the middle of town in summer, for example in the River Aare in Bern.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, clean drinking water comes straight out of the tap. Usually the municipality makes sure of this. It also makes sure that dirty waste water is cleaned in a sewage treatment plant.
wichtigste: The municipality usually takes care of the water supply.
Drinking water comes mainly from springs and groundwater.
The supply is paid for mainly with water charges.
Waste water from the shower and toilet flows into the sewage treatment plant.
There it is cleaned before it goes back into streams and lakes.

abschnitte.text: **Drinking water** in Switzerland comes mostly from **springs** and **groundwater**, and some from lakes. The **municipality** or a group of municipalities runs the pipes, pumps and **reservoirs**. The water is checked regularly. You can drink it without any worries.

The water supply is paid for mainly with **charges**. Anyone who uses a lot of water pays more, because the **water meter** measures how much is used. This follows the **polluter pays principle**. You also pay a separate charge for waste water.

The dirty water from the shower, kitchen and toilet is called **waste water**. It flows through the sewers into a **sewage treatment plant**, also called an **ARA** in Switzerland. There it is cleaned in several stages. Afterwards it may go back into streams, rivers and lakes. The municipalities build and run these plants.

gewusst: Thanks to sewage treatment plants, today you can swim again in many Swiss lakes and rivers, which a few decades ago was often not advisable.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who moves house within Switzerland often changes the place where they pay tax. Then the question arises of where you pay taxes for the year of the move. The answer: what counts is where you live on 31 December.
wichtigste: When you move within Switzerland, what counts is your residence at the end of the tax period.
That is 31 December.
You are taxed at the new place for the whole year.
Anyone who moves from Bern to Lucerne in October pays tax in Lucerne for the whole year.
You have to register with the municipality at the new place.

abschnitte.text: If someone moves from one canton to another, only **one canton** is responsible for the year of the move. What counts is the **residence at the end of the tax period**, in other words on **31 December**. For example, Lea moves from Bern to Lucerne in October. She is taxed in the canton of **Lucerne** for the whole year.

This way you do not have to fill in two tax returns for two cantons. The rule is simple and the same for everyone. It was laid down in the Confederation’s **Tax Harmonisation Act**. When moving within a canton, the place of residence at the end of the year usually applies too.

abschnitte.titel: What do you have to do?
abschnitte.text: After a move, you deregister with the old municipality and register with the new **residents’ registration office**. The tax offices then exchange the information with each other. For the year of the move, you receive the **tax return** from the new canton. Anyone who keeps a house in the old canton continues to pay part of their taxes there for it.

gewusst: Different rules apply to moving abroad or moving from abroad than to moving within Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A tip is a voluntary amount that guests give on top of the price, for example in a restaurant or at the hairdresser’s. For the person who receives it, however, it is income. That is why it is in principle part of taxable income.
wichtigste: A tip is voluntary and a thank you for good service.
In Switzerland, service is usually already included in the price.
For employees, tips are part of their income from work.
That is why tips are taxable in principle.
They are often noted on the salary statement or taken into account in the tax assessment.

abschnitte.text: If you were happy in a restaurant, you often round up the bill. This extra money is called a **tip**. In Switzerland, **service** has long been included in the price, so the tip really is voluntary. It is given in cash or added on when paying by card.

For employees, tips are part of their **income from work**. That is why they are **taxable** in principle, just like wages. They often appear on the **salary statement**, especially when they are distributed through the business. Otherwise the tax office takes them into account in the **tax assessment**. Exactly how this is done can vary slightly from canton to canton.

Anyone who receives a lot of tips should not forget them in their tax return. The tax depends on your total income. Anyone who keeps income quiet risks **back tax** and a fine. If you are unsure, the tax office can help.

gewusst: In some countries, for example in the USA, a large tip is usual because service is not included in the price.
In many restaurants, tips are collected and shared among the whole team.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who starts working will at some point have to pay taxes too. For most people, income tax is not deducted directly from their wages. That is why it is worth putting some money aside for it every month.
wichtigste: For most people in Switzerland, tax is not deducted from their wages.
The tax bill often only arrives months later.
Anyone who saves a little every month will not be caught by surprise.
A separate tax account helps with saving.
Many cantons pay interest if you pay your taxes early.

abschnitte.text: People who are **taxed in the ordinary way** fill in a tax return and then receive a **bill** from the tax office. So the money is not deducted from their wages. The bill can arrive several months after the year in which the wages were earned. Anyone who has not put money aside by then can quickly get into difficulties.

A good tip for **apprentices** and young workers: pay a fixed amount into a separate **tax account** every month. That way the money is ready when the bill arrives. You can estimate how much you should save with the canton’s **tax calculator**. Your **budget** should also include an item for taxes.

In many cantons you can pay your taxes in advance in **instalments**. Anyone who pays early often even receives a little **credit interest** for it. Anyone who pays late, on the other hand, has to pay **default interest**. It is also worth declaring all permitted deductions in your tax return.

gewusst: For people without a Swiss passport and without a settlement permit, tax is often deducted directly from their wages, and this is called withholding tax.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes a sick or injured person has to be transported by ambulance. Basic insurance contributes to these costs, but only up to a certain limit.
wichtigste: Basic insurance contributes to medically necessary transport.
It covers 50 % of the costs, up to a maximum of 500 francs a year.
For rescues it pays 50 %, up to a maximum of 5000 francs a year.
You pay the rest yourself, or supplementary insurance does.
Patient transport can cost several hundred to over a thousand francs.

abschnitte.text: The law distinguishes between two cases. A **transport** is, for example, taking a patient who cannot sit or walk by herself from one hospital to another. A **rescue** is an operation in an emergency, for example after an accident in the mountains or when someone’s life is in danger. Different contributions apply to the two cases.

For **medically necessary transport**, basic insurance pays **half the costs**, but at most **500 francs a year**. For **rescues** it also pays 50 %, at most **5000 francs a year**. The insured person has to bear the rest themselves. Because an operation like this is expensive, that can be a lot of money.

That is why many people have **supplementary insurance** that covers a larger part. Anyone who has an **accident** and is employed is also protected by their employer’s accident insurance. A patron membership of **Rega**, the Swiss Air Rescue, can also help with rescues. Even so: in an emergency, always call 144 straight away, whatever it costs.

gewusst: In Switzerland, Rega flies rescue missions by helicopter, often in the mountains too.
“Medically necessary” means that a journey by car, taxi or train is not possible for health reasons.

teile.einleitung: Food gives the body the energy to grow, play and learn. A healthy diet is varied and colourful. Lots of vegetables, fruit and wholegrain products are part of it, sweet things only now and then.
wichtigste: A healthy plate is **colourful** and varied.
**Vegetables** and **fruit** provide vitamins and minerals.
**Wholegrain products** keep you full for a long time.
The best drink for thirst is **water**.
Sweets and sugary drinks are only for now and then.
The **food pyramid** shows how much of each kind of food you should eat.

abschnitte.text: The body needs energy to move and to think. This energy comes from food. It also needs building blocks such as **protein** for the muscles and **calcium** for the bones. **Vitamins** and **minerals** help everything in the body work well, for example the defences against illness.

The **food pyramid** of the Swiss Society for Nutrition shows what belongs in a healthy diet. At the bottom are drinks, above all water. Above that come vegetables and fruit, then cereal products and potatoes. Further up are dairy products, meat, fish, eggs and tofu. At the very top are sweet and salty things: only a little of these.

A well-known rule is **“5 a day”**: three portions of vegetables and two portions of fruit a day. A portion is about a handful. The more colourful the plate, the more different vitamins you get. **Wholemeal bread** contains more fibre than white bread and keeps you full for longer.

It is best to drink **water** or unsweetened tea. Fizzy and sugary drinks contain a lot of sugar. Too much sugar is bad for your **teeth** and can make you put on weight. That is why sweets are something for special moments. But a piece of chocolate now and then is no problem.

Eating is more than just getting full. At a shared meal with the family or at school, you can talk and enjoy your food. If you eat slowly and chew well, you notice more easily when you are full. **Breakfast** gives you energy for the morning. A healthy **mid-morning snack** helps you stay focused at school.

gewusst: The Swiss food pyramid is not a diet, but a guide for every day.
In the food pyramid, potatoes do not count as vegetables but as starchy side dishes, like bread and pasta.

teile.einleitung: In the sports hall, schoolchildren have PE lessons, and in the evening clubs often train there. It is usually built and equipped by the municipality. The money for it comes mainly from taxes.
wichtigste: The sports hall usually belongs to the school.
State schools are the responsibility of the cantons and municipalities.
New mats and equipment are usually paid for by the municipality with taxes.
In the evening, sports clubs often use the hall.
Good care makes sure that the equipment lasts a long time.

abschnitte.text: PE lessons take place in the **sports hall**. There is equipment such as **mats**, parallel bars, rings, wall bars and balls. In Switzerland, sport is a fixed part of school lessons. Exercise keeps you healthy and is fun.

The sports hall belongs to the **school building**, and the **cantons and municipalities** are responsible for state schools. When new mats are needed, the **municipality** usually pays for them. The money comes from the **taxes** that the people in the municipality pay. Large expenses such as a new sports hall are often decided by voters at the municipal assembly or at the ballot box.

In the evenings and at weekends, **clubs** often train in the hall, for example in gymnastics, volleyball or floorball. Some municipalities charge a small fee for this. In this way, a building that was built with tax money is used by as many people as possible.

gewusst: Many larger sports halls can be divided into two or three smaller halls with partition walls.

teile.einleitung: A pharmacy is a shop where you can get medicines and health products. That is also where you get the medicines that a doctor has prescribed for you. Pharmacists are experts who give good advice and can often help directly with minor complaints.
wichtigste: At the pharmacy you get medicines that a doctor has prescribed.
Many medicines for minor complaints are also available without a prescription.
Pharmacists have completed several years of studying pharmacy.
In Switzerland, a green cross shows that there is a pharmacy.
In every region there is an emergency pharmacy for nights and weekends.
Prescribed medicines are usually paid for by health insurance if they are on the official list.
In some cantons, doctors also hand out medicines directly.

abschnitte.text: A **pharmacy** sells medicines and advises people on health questions. The German word “Apotheke” comes from Greek and originally meant store or storeroom. In Switzerland you can recognise pharmacies by the glowing **green cross**. There are about 1,800 pharmacies in the whole country (as of 2023).

Some medicines are very strong and may only be handed out with a **prescription**. A prescription is a written instruction from the doctor. Other remedies, for example for a sore throat or a runny nose, are available without a prescription after some advice. Very simple products such as plasters or cough sweets can even be found on the shelf.

Anyone who wants to become a pharmacist studies **pharmacy** at a university, for example in Basel, Bern, Geneva or at ETH Zurich. The course takes five years up to the master’s degree. Pharmacists are supported by **pharmacy assistants**, who do an apprenticeship. Today, pharmacists in Switzerland are also allowed to give vaccinations and hand out certain medicines without a doctor’s prescription.

When all pharmacies are closed at night or at the weekend, there is an **emergency service**. Which pharmacy is on duty is shown on the internet, in the newspaper or on the pharmacy door. For minor complaints it is often worth going to the pharmacy first instead of to A&E. The experts also recognise when you really should see a doctor.

Basic insurance pays for medicines that a doctor has prescribed and that are on the Confederation’s **list of specialities**. You pay part of the costs yourself through the deductible and the excess. If there is a cheaper **generic** with the same active ingredient, you have to pay a higher excess for the more expensive original. The pharmacy will advise you about this.

Medicines are not sweets and can be dangerous if used wrongly. That is why they belong in a safe place that small children cannot reach. Out-of-date medicines or ones you no longer need can be taken back to the pharmacy free of charge. There they are disposed of properly so that they do not end up in the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Written instruction from the doctor saying which medicine you should get.
Science of medicines, which pharmacists study.
Cheaper copy of a medicine with the same active ingredient.
Pharmacy that is on duty at night and at weekends.

gewusst: In the past, pharmacists made almost all medicines themselves, such as ointments, syrups and pills from herbs.
In cantons such as Zurich or St Gallen, many family doctors hand out medicines themselves, and this is called self-dispensing.
The Pharmacy Museum of the University of Basel shows an old pharmacy with jars and herbs.

teile.einleitung: The tax multiplier is a figure in per cent by which the basic tax is multiplied. With it, the canton and the municipality determine how much tax you pay in the end. Each municipality sets its own tax multiplier.
wichtigste: The tax multiplier is a percentage.
It is multiplied by the basic tax.
A tax multiplier of 120 per cent means: basic tax times 1.2.
Each municipality decides its own tax multiplier.
It is decided by the municipal assembly, the municipal parliament or the people.
A lower tax multiplier means less municipal tax.
That is why, with the same wage, you often pay a different amount in the neighbouring village.

abschnitte.text: Many cantons first calculate the **basic tax**. It depends on income and is the same throughout the canton. It is then multiplied by the **tax multiplier**. Example: the basic tax is 1000 francs and the municipal tax multiplier is 120 per cent. Then the municipal tax is 1000 times 1.2, which makes **1200 francs**.

The municipality’s tax multiplier is set by the **municipal assembly** or the **municipal parliament**, often together with the budget. Sometimes the people vote on it at the ballot box. The canton also has its own tax multiplier. In this way, the people who live there help decide how much tax they pay.
