If a municipality needs more money, for example for a new **school building**, it can raise the tax multiplier. If it has enough money, it can lower it. If the tax multiplier falls from 100 to 90 per cent, residents pay less **municipal tax**. Direct federal tax and VAT, however, are not affected.

Because each municipality sets its own tax multiplier, taxes differ even within one canton. Two people with exactly the same income therefore do not pay the same amount if they live in different municipalities. That is why some people also look at the tax multiplier when they move house.

gewusst: The tax multiplier can also be over 100 per cent, in which case the tax is higher than the basic tax.
Direct federal tax has no tax multiplier, it is the same throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who wants to change health insurer has to cancel their old basic insurance. Fixed dates apply to this. What matters is when the cancellation reaches the insurer.
wichtigste: The cancellation must reach the insurer in good time.
What counts is when it arrives, not the postmark date.
To cancel at the end of the year, the cancellation must arrive by 30 November.
With a 300-franc deductible and the standard model, you can also cancel at the end of June.
Then the cancellation must arrive by 31 March.
It is safest to send the cancellation by registered post.

abschnitte.titel: Cancelling at the end of the year
abschnitte.text: Most people change insurer with effect from **1 January**. For this, the cancellation must have **arrived** at the old insurer by **30 November** at the latest. If this day falls at a weekend, the last working day before it applies. In autumn the insurers announce their new premiums, which leaves time to compare.

What matters is the **date of arrival** at the health insurer, not the date on which you send the letter. Anyone who posts it on the last day is too late. That is why you send the cancellation early and ideally by **registered post**. With the receipt from the post office you can prove when the letter arrived.

abschnitte.titel: Cancelling at the end of June
abschnitte.text: Anyone who has the **standard deductible** of 300 francs and the **standard model** has a second option. They can also cancel with three months’ notice at the **end of June**. The cancellation must then arrive by **31 March**. Anyone who has chosen a higher deductible or a special model such as the family doctor model can only change at the end of the year.

It is best to sign up with the new insurer first. The old insurance only ends once the new insurer has confirmed that it has accepted you. **Supplementary insurance** is not cancelled automatically at the same time, and it often has its own deadlines.

gewusst: If the insurer raises the premium, you may also cancel at the end of the year with a special model or a higher deductible.
Many insurers offer a template for the cancellation letter, but you can also write it yourself.

teile.einleitung: Being healthy means more than not being ill. You feel good in your body, you are cheerful and you get on well with others. With good habits, everyone can do a lot for their own health.
wichtigste: The **World Health Organization** (WHO) describes health as physical, mental and social well-being.
The WHO has its headquarters in **Geneva**.
Enough **sleep** is very important for children.
**Exercise** and **good food** keep the body fit.
**Hygiene** such as washing your hands protects against illnesses.
Staying healthy is better than getting ill.

abschnitte.text: In 1948 the **World Health Organization** (WHO) described health like this: a state of complete physical, mental and social **well-being**, not just the absence of illness. So health has to do with the body, the mind and living together. The WHO has its headquarters in **Geneva**.

During **sleep** the body recovers. It grows, repairs itself and strengthens its defences. The brain also sorts out what you have learnt during the day. Children need more sleep than adults. Anyone who sleeps too little is tired, finds it harder to concentrate and gets irritable more quickly.

Anyone who **exercises** a lot strengthens their heart, muscles and bones. It is best to play outdoors every day. Added to this is a **balanced diet** with lots of vegetables and fruit. Water is the best drink. Sweet things are only for now and then.

Many illnesses are passed on by **viruses** and **bacteria**. Washing your hands regularly with soap protects against them, especially before eating and after using the toilet. Anyone who coughs or sneezes does so into the crook of their elbow. **Brushing your teeth** in the morning and evening is also part of hygiene.

Part of health is also feeling **emotionally** well. Friends, family and time to play are good for you. If something is getting you down, it helps to talk about it. For children and young people in Switzerland there is advice from **Pro Juventute** on the number **147**.

gewusst: The WHO was founded in 1948. World Health Day is celebrated every year on 7 April.
When washing your hands, you should soap them for about 20 to 30 seconds.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, not everyone pays the same amount of tax, even if they earn the same amount. It depends on where you live. The cantons and municipalities help to decide how high taxes are.
wichtigste: You pay taxes to the Confederation, the canton and the municipality.
Cantons and municipalities set their own tax rates.
That is why taxes are not equally high everywhere.
Federal tax is the same throughout Switzerland.
This is called tax competition.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are three levels of government: the **Confederation**, the **canton** and the **municipality**. All three collect taxes. **Direct federal tax** is the same everywhere. But the cantons and municipalities set their own taxes. This is part of **federalism**.

Many municipalities set a **tax multiplier** every year. It shows what percentage of the basic cantonal tax you pay to the municipality. The tax multiplier is often decided by voters, for example at the **municipal assembly**. Municipalities with a lot of expenses or little income usually have a higher tax multiplier.

Because taxes differ, people speak of **tax competition**. Supporters think it makes municipalities and cantons careful with money. Critics think it leads to big differences between rich and poorer regions. **Fiscal equalisation** between the cantons is meant to reduce these differences.

gewusst: Between two neighbouring municipalities, the difference in taxes can be noticeable, even though they are only a few kilometres apart.

teile.einleitung: Tax progression means that people with a higher income pay a higher percentage in tax. So anyone who earns a lot not only pays more francs, but also a larger share of their income. In Switzerland, the income taxes of the Confederation and the cantons are progressive.
wichtigste: With progression, the tax rate rises with income.
Anyone who earns more pays a higher percentage.
Direct federal tax is strongly progressive and reaches at most 11.5 per cent.
It is based on the idea that everyone should pay according to their economic capacity.
A distinction is made between the average tax rate and the marginal tax rate.
Despite progression, a pay rise always leaves you with more money.
Bracket creep happens when wages only rise because of inflation.

abschnitte.text: The word **progression** comes from the Latin “progressio” and means advancing or increasing. With a progressive tax, the tax rate grows with income. Someone who earns 30,000 francs, for example, pays only a few per cent, while someone who earns 300,000 francs pays a much higher share. The opposite would be a **flat tax**, where everyone pays the same percentage.

Income is divided into bands in your mind. Each band has its own rate, and only the part of the income in the higher band is taxed at a higher rate. The rate for the last franc earned is called the **marginal tax rate**. The **average tax rate**, on the other hand, shows what percentage of the whole income you pay overall.

The Federal Constitution requires everyone to be taxed according to their **economic capacity**. People who earn little need almost everything for rent, food and health insurance. People who earn a lot can give up a larger share without having to do without important things. This is meant to make the tax burden feel fair.

With direct federal tax, people on a small income pay nothing at all, and the top rate is 11.5 per cent. The cantons also have progressive tax scales, but each with its own bands. As an exception, the canton of Uri introduced a flat tax with a fixed rate. The canton of Obwalden once wanted to introduce falling rates for very high incomes, but the Federal Supreme Court banned this in 2007.

If wages only rise because everything is getting more expensive, you still slip into a higher tax band. You then pay a higher percentage even though you cannot afford any more. This problem is called **bracket creep**. That is why the Confederation and many cantons regularly adjust their tax scales to inflation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tax rate rises as income grows.
Tax rate on the last franc earned.
Share of the whole income that is paid as tax.
Higher taxes only because of inflation, without really earning more.

gewusst: In Switzerland, a pay rise never leaves you with less money afterwards.
With direct federal tax, about a third of taxpayers pay no tax or almost none.
VAT is not progressive, because everyone pays the same rate when they shop.

teile.einleitung: Tobacco tax is a special tax on cigarettes and other tobacco products. It is collected by the Confederation. The money goes mainly to the AVS and the disability insurance.
wichtigste: Tobacco tax is a federal tax.
It is charged on cigarettes, cigars and other tobacco.
Its revenue is used for the AVS and the disability insurance.
The tax makes cigarettes more expensive.
Higher prices can help to reduce smoking.

abschnitte.text: **Tobacco tax** is a **consumption tax**. It is included in the price of cigarettes, cigars, fine-cut tobacco and similar goods. The manufacturers and importers pay it to the Confederation and include it in the selling price. So in the end, the buyers pay it. The **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** is responsible for collecting it.

The money from tobacco tax does not go into the general fund. It is used for the **AVS** and the **disability insurance**. The AVS pays pensions to older people, and the disability insurance supports people with a disability. In this way the tax helps to finance these important social insurance schemes.

Smoking is very harmful to **health**. Tobacco tax makes cigarettes more expensive. This brings the state **income** and at the same time can **reduce consumption**. Young people in particular are less likely to start smoking when cigarettes are expensive. That is why taxes like this are sometimes also called steering taxes.

gewusst: A large part of the price of a packet of cigarettes in Switzerland is made up of taxes.

teile.einleitung: Wealth includes everything you own that is worth money, for example money in the bank, shares or a house. In Switzerland you pay wealth tax on it. As a rule, what counts is the amount on 31 December.
wichtigste: Wealth is everything you own that is worth money.
Debts are subtracted from wealth.
Wealth tax is only collected by the cantons and municipalities, not by the Confederation.
What counts is the amount at the end of the tax period, in other words on 31 December.
Up to a tax-free allowance you pay no wealth tax.

abschnitte.text: **Wealth** includes money in your account, cash, **securities** such as shares, but also houses, flats or a car. If you have **debts**, for example a mortgage, they are subtracted. What is left is called **net wealth**. The tax is calculated on this.

For **wealth tax**, what usually counts is the amount at the **end of the tax period**, in other words on **31 December**. In your tax return you state how much money was in your accounts on that day. That is why banks send a confirmation of the account balance at the beginning of the year.

Wealth tax is only collected by the **cantons and municipalities**, and the Confederation has no wealth tax. Each canton sets a **tax-free allowance**. Anyone who owns less pays no wealth tax. The tax rates differ from canton to canton.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries in Europe that still has a wealth tax.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, even a newborn baby needs its own basic insurance. The parents must register it with a health insurer within three months of the birth.
wichtigste: Every baby needs its own basic insurance.
The parents must register it within 3 months.
The baby is then insured backdated to the birth.
The insurer must accept the baby into basic insurance.
A lower premium applies to children.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, every person who lives here must have **basic insurance**. This also applies to **newborn babies**. A baby needs its own insurance, it is not simply covered by the parents’ insurance. Babies often go for check-ups and get vaccinations, so protection is important.

The parents must register their child with a health insurer **within 3 months** of the birth. If they do this in time, the baby is insured **backdated to the birth**. This means that costs from the first days of life are also covered. Many parents sort out the registration early so that nothing is forgotten.

As for everyone else, the **obligation to accept** also applies to babies: every insurer must accept the child into basic insurance. The parents may choose the insurer freely, and it does not have to be the same as their own. A **lower premium** applies to children, and the deductible can be 0 francs.

gewusst: There is no obligation to accept for supplementary insurance, and there the insurer may ask health questions.
The children’s premium applies from the first day of life until the end of the year in which the child turns 18.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, the bike is a popular means of transport for the journey to school, for work and for leisure. So that you can ride safely, good cycle paths are needed. These are usually built by the municipality or the canton with tax money.
wichtigste: Cycle paths are part of the road network.
Municipalities and cantons build most cycle paths.
They are paid for mainly with tax money.
Since 2018, cycle paths have been in the Federal Constitution.
Good cycle paths make traffic safer for everyone.

abschnitte.text: A **bike** needs no petrol, is quiet and keeps you fit. Many children ride to school on one. To make this safe, there are **cycle paths** and **cycle lanes** that are separated from car traffic or marked. A helmet, lights and good brakes are also part of safety.

Cycle paths are part of the **roads**. The **municipality** is responsible for municipal roads, the **canton** for cantonal roads. They plan and build the cycle paths and pay for them with **tax money**. Sometimes the Confederation contributes to larger transport projects in cities and urban areas.

In 2018, the people and the cantons approved a **federal decree on cycle paths**. Since then, the bike has been in the **Federal Constitution** alongside footpaths and hiking trails. This allows the Confederation to set out principles and support the cantons. But the paths are still built mainly by the cantons and municipalities.

gewusst: Red signposts in Switzerland show signposted cycle routes, including over long distances across the whole country.

teile.einleitung: Customs checks goods that come into Switzerland across the border or leave it. It collects customs duties and other charges. The Confederation is responsible, through the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security.
wichtigste: Customs is a matter for the Confederation.
The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security, FOCBS for short, is responsible.
Until 2021 it was called the Federal Customs Administration.
The FOCBS checks goods and collects customs duties and import VAT.
There are duty-free allowances for shopping abroad.

abschnitte.text: **Customs** checks goods at the **border**. It checks whether they may be imported and collects **customs duties** and charges, for example **VAT** on imports. It also looks for forbidden things, such as protected animals or plants. In this way it protects people, animals and the economy.

The **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, **FOCBS** for short, is responsible. Until the end of 2021 it was called the **Federal Customs Administration**. It is part of the Federal Department of Finance. The income from customs duties goes to the **Confederation**. The FOCBS also includes staff who check people at the border.

Anyone who shops abroad may bring a certain amount back **duty-free**. For some goods such as meat or alcohol, separate **duty-free allowances** apply. Anything above that must be **declared** at customs and duty paid on it. With the app “QuickZoll” you can also do this on your mobile phone.

gewusst: Switzerland is not part of the European Union’s customs union, which is why there are still checks on goods at its borders.

teile.einleitung: Medicines help with many illnesses, but they can also do harm if you take them wrongly. That is why there are clear rules about who gives them, how they are stored and when health insurance pays for them.
wichtigste: Children only take medicines when their parents or the doctor give them.
Medicines are kept high up and safely.
Small children easily mistake tablets for sweets.
Basic insurance pays for medicines prescribed by a doctor that are on the list of specialities.
The list of specialities is kept by the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH).
You usually pay for remedies bought over the counter yourself.

abschnitte.text: **Medicines** contain active ingredients that change something in the body. They can relieve pain, bring down a fever or fight germs. But if you take too much or the wrong remedy, it can be dangerous. That is why children only take medicines when their **parents or the doctor** give them.

Small children easily mistake colourful tablets for **sweets**. That is why medicines belong in a **safe place**, high up or in a cupboard that can be locked. You never leave them lying around. Out-of-date medicines are taken back to the pharmacy. In case of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on the number **145**.

**Basic insurance** pays for a medicine if it has been **prescribed by a doctor** and is on the **list of specialities**. This list is kept by the **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)**. A medicine is only put on it if it is effective, appropriate and cost-effective. The deductible and excess apply here too.

Many things can be bought at the pharmacy or chemist’s without a prescription, for example some throat lozenges or creams. You usually pay for these **over-the-counter** remedies yourself. If there is a cheaper **generic** with the same active ingredient as an expensive original medicine, you pay a higher excess for the original.

gewusst: A generic contains the same active ingredient as the original medicine, but is usually cheaper.
Before a medicine may be sold in Switzerland, the authority Swissmedic must approve it.

teile.einleitung: A hospital is a place where sick and injured people are treated. Treatment in hospital is expensive. That is why the health insurance fund and the canton pay for it together.
wichtigste: Doctors, nurses and many other specialists work in a hospital.
Public hospitals are also financed with tax money.
When someone stays in hospital, the health insurance fund and the canton pay together.
Since 2012, the canton has paid at least 55 per cent of inpatient treatment.
The health insurance fund covers the rest, at most 45 per cent.
In Switzerland, every person must have health insurance.

abschnitte.text: A **hospital** is a large building for treating sick and injured people. It has emergency departments, operating theatres and rooms for patients. If someone stays overnight, this is called **inpatient** treatment. If you go home again on the same day, it is **outpatient** treatment. In Switzerland people usually say “Spital”, while in Germany they tend to say “Krankenhaus”.

Hospital treatment costs a lot of money. For an inpatient stay, the **health insurance fund** and the **canton** share the costs. The canton pays at least 55 per cent, the health insurance fund at most 45 per cent. The canton’s money comes from **taxes**. The patient pays a small part herself through the deductible and the excess.

Nora breaks her arm and has to stay in hospital. The hospital sends most of the bill to the health insurance fund and to the canton. For many treatments there are fixed amounts, called **flat-rate payments per case**. This means a broken leg is billed in a similar way in every hospital. Nora does not have to worry about the bill, her parents deal with it.

In Switzerland, the **cantons** are mainly responsible for hospital care. On a **hospital list** they decide which hospitals provide basic care. There are public and private hospitals. There are large university hospitals in Zurich, Bern, Basel, Lausanne and Geneva, for example. Research and training also take place there.

gewusst: The word “Spital” comes from the Latin “hospitalis”, which means hospitable.
In the past, monasteries often looked after the sick, the poor and travellers.

teile.einleitung: The list of securities is part of the tax return. In it you list bank accounts, shares and funds. It is used to calculate wealth tax and to reclaim withholding tax.
wichtigste: Its full name is the list of securities and assets.
You list accounts, shares and funds.
What counts is the amount on 31 December.
Interest and dividends are also declared.
Anyone who declares everything gets the withholding tax back.

abschnitte.text: In the **list of securities and assets** you declare all your **bank accounts**, **shares**, **bonds** and **funds**. For each account you write down the balance on **31 December**. Added to this are the year’s earnings, in other words **interest** and **dividends**. The banks send a tax certificate for this every year.

On a lot of interest and dividends, the Confederation directly deducts **withholding tax** of 35 per cent. Anyone who honestly declares the earnings in the list of securities gets this tax **back** or has it offset. So it is worth not keeping anything quiet. That is exactly what withholding tax is meant to achieve.

The tax office needs the list to calculate your **wealth** and your **income** from earnings. The balance counts towards wealth, the interest towards income. Many cantons offer programs that let you enter the information on the computer.

gewusst: A savings account for children also belongs in a list of securities, usually that of the parents.

teile.einleitung: A fever is not an illness in itself, but a reaction of the body. It raises its temperature to fight germs that cause disease. Usually drinking plenty and resting help.
wichtigste: With a **fever**, the body temperature is higher than normal.
People usually speak of a fever from about **38 degrees**.
Fever helps the body fight **viruses** and **bacteria**.
With a fever, the body needs **rest** and plenty of **fluids**.
If the fever lasts a long time or is very high, ask the doctor.

abschnitte.text: Normal body temperature is about **37 degrees**. When we are ill, the body can raise its temperature. From about 38 degrees, this is called a **fever**. It is measured with a **thermometer**. A fever often comes together with a cold or flu.

abschnitte.titel: Why the body makes a fever
abschnitte.text: Fever is part of the body’s **defences**. Many germs do not like the extra warmth and multiply less well. At the same time, the **immune system** works faster. So fever is actually a sign that the body is fighting back. But you often feel weak, and you feel cold or sweat.

With a fever, the body above all needs **rest**. You stay at home and sleep a lot. Because you sweat when you have a fever, the body loses water. That is why **drinking plenty** is important, for example water or tea. Cool cloths on the forehead can feel nice. Medicines for fever are only given after talking to adults or the doctor.

abschnitte.titel: When to go to the doctor?
abschnitte.text: Usually a fever goes away by itself after a few days. Ask the **doctor** if the fever is very high or lasts several days. You should also get medical advice if someone is hardly drinking, is very tired or has other severe complaints. In **babies**, fever must be taken especially seriously.

gewusst: Body temperature is usually a little lower in the morning than in the evening.
Animals can also get a fever, for example dogs and cats.

teile.einleitung: A home first aid kit is a small collection of medicines and aids for use at home. It helps with small injuries and minor illnesses. It is important that it is stored safely and out of reach of small children.
wichtigste: A **home first aid kit** should contain, for example, **plasters**, **bandages** and a **thermometer**.
It helps with small injuries and minor aches and pains.
The home first aid kit is kept somewhere **cool**, **dry** and out of children’s reach.
You check the **expiry date** regularly.
Old medicines are taken back to the **pharmacy**.
You put important **emergency numbers** in the home first aid kit.

abschnitte.text: A home first aid kit includes **plasters** in different sizes, **bandages**, a pair of scissors and tweezers. Added to this are a **disinfectant** for wounds and a **thermometer**. Often there are also remedies for pain and fever, a cream for insect bites and a cooling compress. You can ask at the pharmacy exactly what a family needs.

Medicines are **not toys**. That is why the home first aid kit is kept in a place that small children cannot reach, ideally in a cupboard that can be locked. The place should be **cool** and **dry**. The bathroom is not ideal because of the damp from the shower. Always keep the **package leaflet** with the medicines.

At least once a year, you go through the home first aid kit. Medicines have an **expiry date**. After that, they may no longer work properly. Old medicines or ones you no longer need are not thrown in the bin but taken back to the **pharmacy** or chemist’s. If something is missing, you buy more.

Put a note with important **phone numbers** in the home first aid kit: ambulance 144, Tox Info Suisse 145 and your family doctor’s number. The home first aid kit only helps with small problems. For serious injuries or if you are unsure, get medical help.

gewusst: In Switzerland a first aid kit is recommended in the car, and in some neighbouring countries it is compulsory.
Heat and damp can make medicines go off more quickly.

teile.einleitung: A **playground** in the park is a place for sliding, swinging and climbing. Public playgrounds are usually built and looked after by the municipality. The money for this comes from taxes.
wichtigste: Public playgrounds usually belong to the municipality.
The municipality pays for building and upkeep with tax money.
All children may use them free of charge.
Play equipment must meet strict safety rules.
There is soft impact protection under the equipment.
The municipality checks the playgrounds regularly.

abschnitte.text: At the **playground** there are slides, swings, sandpits and climbing frames. Children meet there, play together and get exercise. Parents and grandparents also find benches to rest on. Because a public playground belongs to everyone, every child may use it **free of charge**.

Usually the **municipality** builds the public playgrounds. It pays for the equipment, the ground and the upkeep with **tax money**. The municipality's gardeners mow the grass, empty the bins and top up the sand. Sometimes neighbourhood associations or donations also help to make a playground nicer.

Play equipment must be built so that children do not easily get hurt. For this there are European **standards**, meaning exact rules. Under slides and swings there is **impact protection** made of sand, wood chips or rubber. The municipality has the equipment **checked** regularly. The **BFU** gives advice on how to make playgrounds safe.

Many new playgrounds look different from in the past. Instead of only metal equipment, there are **tree trunks**, stones, streams and mounds. Such **natural playgrounds** stimulate the imagination. Trees provide shade so that it does not get too hot in summer. Children are often allowed to have a say in the planning.

gewusst: Many playgrounds in Switzerland are also built to be accessible to children in wheelchairs.
In the evenings and at weekends, many school playgrounds are also used as public playgrounds.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes you disagree with a decision by your health insurer. Then you can defend yourself. You lodge an objection against a ruling, and the insurer has to check its decision again.
wichtigste: A **ruling** is a written, official decision by the health insurer.
You can lodge an **objection** against a ruling.
The deadline is stated in the ruling and is usually **30 days**.
It is best to make the objection in writing and give your reasons.
If you also disagree with the decision on the objection, you can go to court.

abschnitte.text: If the health insurer refuses to pay for something, it often first says so in a simple letter. If you disagree, you can ask for a **ruling**. This is an official decision with reasons. At the end there is a **notice of rights of appeal**. It explains how you can challenge the decision and by when.

You send the **objection** to the health insurer that issued the ruling. The deadline is usually **30 days**. You write which decision you disagree with and why. Documents help, for example a report from the doctor. It is best to send the objection by registered post so that you can prove it was sent.

The health insurer checks its decision again and writes a **decision on the objection**. The objection procedure is usually free of charge. If you still disagree, you can lodge an **appeal** with the cantonal insurance court. If you are unsure, you can get advice beforehand from the **health insurance ombudsman**.

gewusst: The deadlines and rules for objections are set out in the Federal Act on the General Part of Social Insurance Law.
The ombudsman mediates between insured people and health insurers, but cannot make decisions.

teile.einleitung: Taxpayers are all the people and companies that pay taxes. Adults who earn money pay part of their wages as taxes. But children also pay a tax when they go shopping: VAT.
wichtigste: Adults who receive wages pay taxes on their wages.
Part of the wages goes to the municipality, the canton and the Confederation.
Anyone who earns more pays more tax.
Children do not fill in their own tax return, the adults do that.
Everyone pays VAT when they go shopping.
Companies are taxpayers too.

abschnitte.text: People who work receive **wages**. They give part of them as **taxes** to the municipality, the canton and the Confederation. For this, adults fill in a **tax return** every year. The money pays for things for everyone, for example schools, roads and hospitals.

abschnitte.titel: Those who have more pay more
abschnitte.text: Anyone who earns more pays more tax. With higher incomes, even the **percentage** rises, and this is called **progression**. People who earn very little often pay hardly any income tax or none at all. In this way, each person contributes to the state according to their means.

Children with **pocket money** do not have to fill in a tax return, the adults do that. Even so, children pay taxes too: the price of every ice cream and every exercise book includes **VAT**. The shop passes it on to the Confederation. Taxes like this that are included in the price are called **indirect taxes**.

It is not only people who pay taxes. **Companies** also pay taxes on their **profit** and their **capital**. Large companies are important taxpayers for many municipalities and cantons. In tax language, companies are called **legal persons** and people are called **natural persons**.

gewusst: In Switzerland, people with high incomes pay a large part of direct federal tax.
Pensioners also pay taxes, for example on their AVS pension.

teile.einleitung: When you apply for supplementary insurance, the health insurer asks health questions. You must answer these truthfully. Anyone who keeps an illness quiet risks the contract being cancelled and the insurance not paying.
wichtigste: There are **health questions** when you apply for **supplementary insurance**.
You must answer them **fully and honestly**.
If you keep something quiet, this is called a **breach of the duty of disclosure**.
The insurer may then withdraw from the contract and refuse to pay.
There are no health questions in **basic insurance**.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who takes out supplementary insurance has a **duty of disclosure**. This means: you must answer the insurer’s questions about your own health correctly and fully. You are asked, for example, about previous illnesses, accidents, operations or medicines. But you only have to state what you are asked about.

If you keep an illness quiet or give false information, this is a **breach of the duty of disclosure**. If the insurer finds out, it may **cancel** the contract. It then does not have to pay for claims connected with the illness you kept quiet. In some circumstances it can ask for money already paid to be returned. That is why honesty always pays.

Read each question carefully and take your time. If you are unsure, you can look at old medical reports or ask your **family doctor**. If you have misunderstood a question, tell the insurer as quickly as possible. Keep a copy of the completed application in a safe place. These rules are set out in the **Insurance Contract Act**.

gewusst: For basic insurance, the obligation to accept applies: the insurer must accept everyone and may not ask health questions.
The insurer can also exclude an illness from supplementary insurance with a reservation.

teile.einleitung: Glasses help people who cannot see clearly. In Switzerland, the basic insurance of the health insurance fund pays a contribution towards glasses for children and young people. For adults, this only applies in special cases.
wichtigste: **Glasses** correct problems with eyesight using specially ground lenses.
For children and young people up to 18, basic insurance pays a **contribution** towards glasses or contact lenses.
This requires a **doctor’s prescription**.
For healthy adults, basic insurance usually pays nothing towards glasses.
For certain eye diseases, it also pays for adults.
**Supplementary insurance** can cover part of the cost of glasses.

abschnitte.text: With an eyesight problem, light does not land exactly on the **retina** in the eye. That is why the image looks blurred. The **lenses** of the glasses bend the light so that the image becomes clear again. For short-sighted and long-sighted people, the lenses are ground differently. The strength of the lenses is measured in **dioptres**.

For children and young people up to their 18th birthday, **basic insurance** pays a fixed contribution towards glasses or contact lenses. It does not cover the whole price, however. The glasses must be **prescribed** by a doctor. That is why you have your eyes examined first, for example by the eye doctor.

For healthy adults, basic insurance **usually does not** pay for new lenses. There is only a contribution for certain diseases or after certain eye operations. That is why many adults have **supplementary insurance** that covers part of the costs. Otherwise you pay for the glasses yourself.

Glasses should fit well and not pinch. The **optician** fits them and straightens them if they are bent. It is best to clean the lenses with a soft cloth so that they do not get scratched. For sport there are special sports glasses. In children, eyesight is checked regularly, because the eyes change as they grow.

gewusst: Glasses have existed since the Middle Ages. The first reading glasses were made in Italy in the 13th century.
Sunglasses protect the eyes from strong light, for example when skiing in the snow.

teile.einleitung: **Service pay**, called “Sold” in German, is the money that members of the army receive per day of service. In Switzerland it is tax-free. The income compensation (EO), which replaces wages, must however be taxed.
wichtigste: Service pay is a small amount per day of military service.
There is also service pay in civil protection.
Service pay is tax-free.
The income compensation scheme, EO for short, replaces part of your wages during service.
The EO is taxable, because it replaces wages.
Pay in the volunteer fire service is also tax-free up to a certain amount.

abschnitte.text: Anyone in Switzerland who does **military service** receives **service pay** for each day of service. The amount is not high. It depends on **rank**, meaning the position you have in the army. Service pay is not a real wage but more like pocket money. The army pays for food, accommodation and equipment.

**Service pay** for military service and civil protection service is **tax-free**. You do not have to declare it as income in your tax return. This is laid down in the Federal Act on Direct Federal Tax and also applies to the cantons. In this way service for the country is not taxed on top.

During service, many people cannot work and earn no wages. That is why there is the **income compensation scheme**, **EO** for short. It pays part of the wages you miss. Because the EO **replaces wages**, it is **taxable**. So it must be declared in the tax return. The EO is paid for through contributions from wages, similar to the AVS.

Firefighters in a **volunteer fire service** also receive pay. For federal tax, it is tax-free up to a certain annual amount. Anyone who does **civilian service** instead of military service also receives EO. Anyone who does no service at all normally pays a **military service exemption tax**.

gewusst: The German word “Sold” is very old and is related to the word “Soldat”, meaning soldier.
The roots of the EO go back to the time of the Second World War, when soldiers were compensated for their lost wages.

teile.einleitung: A children’s hospital is a hospital that is only for children and young people. Experts work here who know a lot about sick and injured children.
wichtigste: A children’s hospital is only for children and young people.
All the experts there specialise in children.
There are playrooms and often school lessons too.
Parents may accompany their children and can often stay overnight there too.
In Switzerland there are children’s hospitals, for example, in Zurich, Basel and St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: In a **children’s hospital**, sick and injured children are treated, from babies to teenagers. The doctors, nurses and therapists specialise in **children**. The equipment, beds and medicines are also suited to small bodies. There is an emergency department, operating theatres and wards for many different illnesses.

A stay in hospital can be difficult for children. That is why children’s hospitals have **playrooms**, colourful rooms and people who play and do crafts with the children. Anyone who has to stay longer often gets **lessons** at the hospital school, so that they do not miss too much at school. Parents may visit their child and can often stay overnight with them too.

There are large children’s hospitals, for example, in **Zurich**, **Basel** and **St Gallen**. Other large hospitals, such as in Bern, Geneva or Lausanne, also have their own children’s clinics. Rare and serious illnesses are treated there too. Most of the costs are covered by health insurance.

In many Swiss children’s hospitals, **hospital clowns** visit the children. They make the children laugh and take their minds off pain and worries. Laughing and playing help many children feel better.

gewusst: Zurich Children’s Hospital was founded in the 19th century and is one of the largest children’s hospitals in Switzerland.
The hospital clowns of the Theodora Foundation are also called “dream doctors”.

teile.einleitung: Almost every year, health insurance premiums are set anew, and they often become more expensive. Insurers must announce the new premiums in good time. This gives insured people time to compare and perhaps change insurer.
wichtigste: Insurers must announce new premiums at least two months in advance.
The new premiums apply from 1 January, so the notification comes by the end of October.
You can cancel basic insurance until 30 November.
The cancellation must have reached the insurer by then.
Premiums rise mainly because health costs rise.
The Federal Office of Public Health checks and approves the premiums.

abschnitte.text: Premiums have to cover the costs of doctors, hospitals and medicines. When these **health costs** rise, premiums usually rise too. Reasons include people living longer and new, expensive treatments becoming available. Insurers may not simply set premiums themselves. The **Federal Office of Public Health** checks and approves them.

Insurers must announce new premiums **at least two months** before they take effect. Because the new premiums apply from **1 January**, the letter arrives by the **end of October** at the latest. In autumn, newspapers and television also report on the new premiums. That is a good moment to check your own insurance.

Anyone who wants to change insurer cancels their basic insurance by **30 November**. The cancellation must have **arrived** at the insurer by then, so it is sent early and ideally by registered post. At the same time you sign up with the new insurer. In basic insurance, all insurers pay for the same services. So changing can save money without you being less well insured.

You do not necessarily have to change insurer to save money. You can also choose a higher **deductible** or a different **insurance model**, for example the family doctor model. You should think carefully about how much you expect to spend on doctors. Anyone with little money can apply to the canton for a **premium reduction**.

gewusst: Changing insurer in basic insurance does not change the services, because they are laid down by law and are the same for everyone.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who breaks a bone often gets a plaster cast. It keeps the broken bone still so that it can grow back together properly. After a few weeks the cast is removed again.
wichtigste: A **plaster cast** keeps a broken bone still.
This allows the **bone** to grow back together.
With an **X-ray**, the doctor can see whether and how the bone is broken.
Today a light **synthetic cast** is often used too.
In children, broken bones usually heal faster than in adults.
A cast must not get wet and must not press.

abschnitte.text: In a fall, for example from a bike or on the ski slope, a bone can break. This is called a **broken bone** or a **fracture**. The arm or leg then hurts a lot and swells up. In hospital or at the doctor’s surgery, an **X-ray** is taken. It shows where and how the bone is broken.

A bone can **grow back together** by itself. For this, the two broken pieces must be in the right position and stay **still**. That is exactly what the cast does. It surrounds the arm or leg like a firm shell. In children the bone has often healed after just a few weeks, while in adults it usually takes longer.

The classic cast is made of plaster from the mineral **gypsum**, which is mixed with water and then becomes hard. Today there is often a **synthetic cast**. It is lighter, sturdier and sometimes even coloured. Many children let their friends draw on the cast or sign it. That makes the time in a cast a bit more fun.

A cast must **not get wet**, so you protect it with a cover in the shower. You do not stick anything inside it, even if it itches. If the cast hurts a lot, presses or the fingers turn cold and blue, you must go to the doctor straight away. After the cast is removed, the muscle is often weak, but with exercise it becomes strong again.

gewusst: An X-ray shows bones as bright, because they block X-rays more than skin and muscles do.
An adult human has about 206 bones.

teile.einleitung: Takeaway means food to take with you. For VAT, it makes a difference whether you take the food away or eat it on the spot. For takeaway, the reduced rate usually applies, and in a restaurant the standard rate.
wichtigste: Takeaway means food to take with you.
Food to take away usually falls under the reduced VAT rate.
Since 2024 the reduced rate has been 2.6 per cent.
Anyone who eats in a restaurant pays the standard rate.
Since 2024 the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent.

abschnitte.text: If you buy a sandwich to **take away**, this counts as a **supply of food**. The **reduced VAT rate** of 2.6 per cent applies to it. If you sit down and eat on the premises, it is a **catering service**. Then the **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent applies. Both rates have applied since 2024.

In a restaurant you get more than just food. You have a table and crockery, and you are served. This counts as a **service**. Food, on the other hand, is an everyday necessity. That is why it is taxed at a lower rate, so that food remains affordable for everyone.

At many snack stalls the staff ask: “To take away or to eat here?” This is also important because of VAT. On the receipt you can see which rate was charged. Often the price for customers is still the same, and the business bears the difference.

gewusst: In Switzerland there is a separate special VAT rate for overnight stays in hotels, which has been 3.8 per cent since 2024.

teile.einleitung: The premium is the amount you pay to the health insurer regularly, usually every month. You always pay it, even if you stay healthy all year. In return you are insured if you fall ill or have an accident.
wichtigste: You usually pay the premium to the health insurer every month.
You pay it even if you stay healthy all year.
The amount depends on the insurer, where you live, your age, the deductible and the insurance model.
Health and sex play no part in basic insurance.
For children, the parents pay the premium, which is much lower than for adults.
The new premiums are announced each autumn.
Anyone who does not pay receives reminders and may face debt enforcement.

abschnitte.text: The **premium** is the price of insurance cover. You pay it regularly, usually **every month**. All insured people pay into a shared fund. Anyone who falls ill gets money from it for the doctor, hospital or medicines. That is why you pay the premium even if you never went to the doctor all year.

The premium depends on the **health insurer**, **where you live**, your **age**, the **deductible** and the **insurance model**. Your state of health plays no part in basic insurance. Your **sex** does not count either. If two people have the same insurer, the same place of residence, the same age, the same deductible and the same model, they pay the same amount. The premium also does not depend on income.

For **children**, the parents take out the insurance and pay the premium. Children’s premiums are much **lower** than adults’ premiums. Young adults up to 25 also usually pay a bit less. Families with little money can get a **premium reduction** from the canton. For children this help is especially large.

The new premiums for the next year are announced each **autumn**. The Federal Office of Public Health checks and approves them beforehand. After that there is time to compare premiums. You can change insurer for the next year until the **end of November**. In basic insurance, all insurers pay for the same services.

Basic insurance remains compulsory even if you do not pay the premium. The insurer then sends **reminders**. It can also claim the money through **debt enforcement proceedings**. But it may not cancel the basic insurance. Anyone who has trouble paying the premium should look for help early.

gewusst: In basic insurance, a person who is ill pays the same premium as a healthy person.
The premium does not depend on wages. That is why the canton helps people with little money through the premium reduction.

teile.einleitung: Some things in the home can be poisonous, for example cleaning products, medicines or certain plants. They do not belong in children’s hands. If something does happen, the emergency number 145 helps in Switzerland.
wichtigste: **Poison** is a substance that can harm the body.
**Cleaning products**, **medicines** and some **plants** can be poisonous.
Poisonous things are stored safely and out of children’s reach.
**Hazard symbols** on the packaging warn of dangerous substances.
In case of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** helps on the number **145**.
If someone is unconscious or has trouble breathing, call **144** straight away.

abschnitte.text: In every home there are things that can be poisonous. These include **cleaning products**, washing powder, descaler or lamp oil. **Medicines** can also be dangerous if you take too much of them. Some **plants** and berries in the garden or in the woods are poisonous too. That is why you do not eat anything that you do not know for sure.

**Hazard symbols** are printed on dangerous products. They are diamonds with a red border and a black picture, for example a skull or a hand being attacked by a liquid. They show that the contents are poisonous, corrosive or flammable. Children should learn early on: bottles like these are **not toys**.

Cleaning products and medicines are kept **high up** or in a cupboard that can be locked. You never pour them into drinks bottles, so that nobody mixes them up. Many bottles have a **child-resistant cap**. It is hard to open, but not impossible. That is why you still have to be very careful.

If someone has swallowed something poisonous, fetch an **adult** straight away. The emergency number **145** of **Tox Info Suisse** gives information around the clock. Take the packaging with you to the phone. If the person is unconscious or has trouble breathing, call the ambulance on **144** straight away.

gewusst: Whether something is poisonous often depends on the amount. The doctor Paracelsus already said, more or less: the dose makes the poison.
Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich and answers many thousands of enquiries every year.

teile.einleitung: Sneezing is a reflex: with it, the body forcefully expels dust, pollen or germs from the nose. Many small droplets fly through the air as you do so. That is why it is important to sneeze properly.
wichtigste: Sneezing is a protective reflex of the nose.
When you sneeze, many tiny droplets fly through the air.
Illnesses such as colds or flu can be passed on with these droplets.
It is best to sneeze into the crook of your arm, at your elbow.
Afterwards, and after blowing your nose, you should wash your hands.
Used tissues belong in the bin straight away.

abschnitte.text: Sneezing is a **reflex**. This means the body does it by itself, and you can hardly stop it. When something irritates the lining of the nose, for example dust, pollen or germs, the brain sends a signal. Then you take a deep breath and push it out through your nose and mouth with great force. This cleans the nose. You also often have to sneeze when you have a cold or **hay fever**.

When you sneeze, many tiny **droplets** fly through the air. They can contain viruses or bacteria. If another person breathes them in, they can become ill. This is called **droplet infection**. This is how colds and flu spread, for example.

It is best to sneeze or cough into the **crook of your arm**, at your elbow. That way the germs spread less, and your hands stay cleaner. If you sneeze into your hands, you pass the germs on with the next handshake or on the door handle. You can also sneeze into a **tissue** and throw it away straight afterwards. It is also good to turn away from other people when you sneeze.

After sneezing or blowing your nose, you should **wash your hands**. With water and **soap**, many germs are removed. Rub every part, including between the fingers. Anyone who is ill is best off staying at home and recovering. That way you also protect the others at school or at work.

gewusst: Most people close their eyes automatically when they sneeze.
Some people have to sneeze when they suddenly look into bright light. This is called the photic sneeze reflex.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Health Insurance Act, KVG for short, governs compulsory basic insurance in Switzerland. It states that all people who live in Switzerland must be insured against illness. The law has applied since 1996 and determines which services health insurers have to pay for.
wichtigste: The KVG is the law that governs basic insurance.
All people who live in Switzerland must be insured against illness.
The people approved the KVG in 1994, and it has been in force since 1 January 1996.
In basic insurance, health insurers must accept everyone.
All insurers pay for the same services in basic insurance.
People who earn little receive a premium reduction from the canton.
Supplementary insurance is voluntary and is not covered by the KVG.

abschnitte.text: The **Health Insurance Act** is a federal law that governs health insurance throughout Switzerland. It determines who has to be insured, what is insured and how the costs are shared. Insurance under the KVG is called **basic insurance** or compulsory health care insurance. The Federal Office of Public Health, FOPH for short, is responsible for supervision.

Before the KVG, health insurance was voluntary in most cantons. Many people were not insured, and insurers could turn down people who were ill or older. On 4 December 1994, voters narrowly approved the new law. Since 1 January 1996, **compulsory insurance** has applied to everyone.

In basic insurance, every health insurer must accept everyone, no matter how old or ill they are. All insurers pay for the same services, for example visits to the doctor, hospital stays and prescribed medicines. Within one region, adults with the same insurer pay the same **premium**, regardless of their state of health. In basic insurance, insurers may not make a profit.

As well as the monthly premium, insured people pay part of the costs themselves. First comes the **deductible**, which for adults is at least 300 francs and at most 2,500 francs a year. After that, you pay 10 per cent of the costs as the **excess**, up to a maximum of 700 francs a year. For children the share of costs is lower, and their deductible is often zero francs.

Premiums have risen sharply in recent years and are a burden for many families. That is why people on a low income receive a **premium reduction** from the Confederation and the cantons. Each canton decides for itself how much people get. For children and young adults in education or training, premiums are reduced especially strongly.

What is not in the KVG can be covered voluntarily with **supplementary insurance**. This includes, for example, a single room in hospital, braces for teeth or alternative treatments. Supplementary insurance is governed by a different law, the Insurance Contract Act. Here, insurers may ask health questions and may also turn people down.

begriffe.erklaerung: Compulsory health insurance that everyone in Switzerland must have.
Amount you pay every month for health insurance.
Amount you first pay yourself each year before the insurer pays.
Share of the costs that you bear yourself after the deductible.
Obligation that applies to everyone, here the obligation to be insured.

gewusst: Anyone who moves to Switzerland must take out health insurance within three months.
You may change your basic insurance every year, and the new insurer has to accept you.
A baby can be registered with a health insurer even before it is born.

teile.einleitung: A grant is money that someone receives for their education and does not have to pay back. In Switzerland, it is mainly the cantons that award these education grants. Grants from public funds are usually tax-free.
wichtigste: A grant helps to pay for education or training.
It does not have to be paid back.
In Switzerland, the cantons are mainly responsible for this.
Whether you get one depends on your family’s income.
Grants from public funds are usually tax-free.

abschnitte.text: Education costs money, for example for materials, books, travel or accommodation. Not every family can pay for this alone. A **grant** is a contribution that you **do not have to pay back**. There are also **education loans**, which you have to pay back later. Together, both are called **education contributions**.

In Switzerland, the **cantons** are mainly responsible. You submit an application to the canton where your parents live. It checks how much the family earns and how much the education costs. There are grants, for example, for an **apprenticeship**, **upper secondary school** and **university**. Foundations sometimes award grants too.

Grants from public funds count as **support** and are usually **tax-free**. So you do not have to pay income tax on them. Often, however, you still declare them in your tax return. This way the tax office can see where the money comes from.

gewusst: The German word for grant, “Stipendium”, comes from Latin and originally meant a soldier’s pay or wages.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is employed in Switzerland is insured against accidents through their employer, including in their free time. When the job ends, this protection also ends after a short time. With extended accident cover you can extend it.
wichtigste: Employees are insured under the Accident Insurance Act, the UVG.
From eight hours a week, this also applies to accidents in your free time.
After a job ends, this protection continues for another 31 days.
With extended accident cover you can extend it by up to 6 months.
It must be taken out before the protection ends.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, employers must insure their employees against accidents. This is set out in the **Accident Insurance Act**, **UVG** for short. There is **occupational accident insurance** for accidents at work. Anyone who works at least eight hours a week for one employer is also insured against **non-occupational accidents**. These are accidents in your free time, for example while skiing.

When a job ends, you are not immediately without protection. Insurance against accidents in your free time continues for another **31 days**. This is called **follow-on cover**. After that it ends if you do not have a new job. Without accident cover through an employer, you have to include accident cover with your **health insurance**.

With **extended accident cover** you can extend the cover for accidents in your free time by up to **6 months**. This is useful, for example, for a longer journey, a language stay abroad or between two jobs. You take it out with your previous employer’s accident insurer, often **Suva**. It is important to take it out and pay for it before the follow-on cover ends.

gewusst: The benefits of accident insurance under the UVG are often better than accident cover through health insurance.
In German, the insurance is called “Abredeversicherung” because you “abreden”, in other words agree, it with the insurer.

teile.einleitung: Colds and flu often pass from person to person. People infect each other. With a few simple rules you can protect yourself and others.
wichtigste: Colds are usually caused by viruses.
Germs reach other people through droplets and through the hands.
Sneezing and coughing into the crook of your elbow helps to protect others.
Washing your hands regularly with soap is very effective.
Anyone who is ill is best off staying at home and resting.

abschnitte.text: Colds are usually caused by **viruses**. When you sneeze, cough or speak, tiny **droplets** fly through the air. If someone breathes them in, they can catch the illness. This is called **droplet infection**. Germs also stick to hands, door handles or keyboards. If you then touch your mouth, nose or eyes, they get into your body. This is a **contact infection**.

Anyone who has to sneeze or cough is best off doing it into the **crook of their elbow** or into a tissue. That way fewer droplets fly through the air, and your hands stay clean. Used tissues should go straight into a bin. Anyone who sneezes into their hands later spreads the germs on everything they touch.

**Washing your hands** is one of the best ways to avoid infection. You wash your hands with **soap** and rub them for about 20 to 30 seconds, including between the fingers. Then rinse and dry them well. It is important after blowing your nose, after going to the toilet, before eating and when you come home.

Anyone who has a fever or feels very ill is best off staying at home. That way you do not infect anyone at school or at work. The body can recover in peace. Airing rooms regularly helps, because fresh air reduces the number of germs in the room. There is also a **vaccination** against some illnesses, such as flu.

gewusst: Colds can be caused by over a hundred different viruses. That is why there is no vaccine against the common cold.
Antibiotics do not help against viruses, only against bacteria.

teile.einleitung: Between the ages of 19 and 25, you belong to the group of young adults with your health insurer. They have their own premiums, which are usually lower than for older adults.
wichtigste: The children’s premium applies up to 18.
From the year in which you turn 19, you pay the premium for young adults.
This premium is higher than the children’s premium, but usually lower than from 26.
From 19, the deductibles for adults apply, from 300 to 2500 francs.
Young adults in education or training often receive a premium reduction.
During this time, many become responsible for their own health insurance.

abschnitte.text: Health insurers divide insured people into three age groups: **children** up to 18, **young adults** from 19 to 25 and **adults** from 26. What counts is your year of birth: from the year in which you turn 19, you move into the new group. The services of basic insurance stay exactly the same, only the premium changes.

The premium for young adults is **higher than the children’s premium**, but usually lower than the premium from 26. In addition, the rules for adults now apply: the **deductible** is between 300 and 2500 francs. The **excess** is 10 % of the costs and at most 700 francs a year. Anyone who is rarely ill should check whether a higher deductible is cheaper.

Many young people are still doing an apprenticeship or studying and earn little. That is why the cantons pay **premium reductions** to people on a low income. For young adults in education or training, the law provides for a special reduction. Each canton decides for itself how to apply for it.

At 18 you come of age and can sign your own contracts. Many now take over their health insurance themselves, even if their parents may still be paying. Anyone who works and is employed for at least eight hours a week is **insured against accidents** through their employer. Then you can exclude accident cover from your health insurance and save on the premium.

gewusst: The amount of the premium depends not only on age, but also on the canton and the premium region you live in.
At 26 you automatically move into the adult group.

teile.einleitung: The health insurance premium also depends on where you live. Some cantons are divided into premium regions for this purpose. This means you can pay different amounts within the same canton and with the same insurer.
wichtigste: A premium region is an area with its own premium level.
A canton can be divided into up to three premium regions.
Some cantons have only one single premium region.
In cities, health costs and therefore premiums are often higher than in the countryside.
Anyone who moves within the canton may therefore get a different premium.

abschnitte.text: A **premium region** is an area in which the same premium level applies. Some cantons are divided into **up to three** premium regions. Other cantons form just one single region. The **Confederation** decides which municipality belongs to which region. Each insurer has its own premiums for each region.

In **cities**, health costs are often higher than in the **countryside**. There are more hospitals and doctors’ surgeries there, for example, and people go to them more often. That is why premiums in cities are usually a bit more expensive. Anyone who lives in a village in the same canton often pays less. The differences between the cantons are even bigger.

Anyone who moves tells the health insurer their new **address**. If the new place of residence is in a different premium region or a different canton, the premium changes. That is why you always enter your own place of residence when **comparing premiums**. That way you see the premiums that apply exactly there.

gewusst: Two people with the same insurer, the same age and the same deductible can pay different premiums in the same canton, just because they live in different municipalities.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is ill pays part of the treatment costs themselves, even though they pay premiums. This share is called cost sharing. It is made up of the deductible, the excess and the contribution to hospital stays.
wichtigste: Cost sharing includes the deductible, the excess and the hospital contribution.
The premium is not part of it, it is the price of the insurance.
First you pay the deductible entirely yourself.
After that you pay a 10 % excess.
For adults, the excess is limited to 700 francs a year.
Cost sharing is meant to help avoid unnecessary visits to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: **Cost sharing** is the share of the treatment costs that insured people bear themselves. It is made up of three parts: the **deductible**, the **excess** and the **hospital contribution** for a stay in hospital. The **premium** is not part of it. You pay that every month, whether you are ill or not.

The **deductible** is a fixed amount per year that you first pay entirely yourself. Adults choose between 300 and 2500 francs. Example: Luca has a deductible of 2500 and a bill of 1800 francs. Because that is below the deductible, he pays everything himself and the insurer pays nothing. Anyone who chooses a high deductible pays a lower premium in return.

Once the deductible has been reached, you still pay a **10 % excess** on the further costs. Example: Mia has a deductible of 300 and a bill of 500 francs. She pays 300 francs deductible and 10 % of 200 francs, in other words 20 francs, making 320 francs in total. For adults, the excess is limited to **700 francs** a year. With a deductible of 2500 you therefore pay at most 3200 francs, not counting the hospital contribution.

Often the insurer first pays a bill in full, for example at the hospital or the pharmacy. This is called **tiers payant**. Afterwards it claims the deductible and excess from the insured person. That is why a bill from the insurer can still arrive months after a visit to the doctor.

Anyone who pays part themselves is more likely to think about whether a visit to the doctor is really necessary. This is meant to help keep **health costs**, and therefore premiums, lower. For children, cost sharing is lower: their excess is limited to 350 francs a year.

gewusst: The hospital contribution does not apply to children and young adults in education or training.
The deductible starts again from the beginning every year on 1 January.

teile.einleitung: Tax evasion means that someone does not declare income or wealth and therefore pays too little tax. This is forbidden and unfair to everyone else. If it is discovered, you have to pay what is owed and also pay a fine.
wichtigste: Tax evasion means not declaring income or wealth.
It can happen deliberately or through negligence.
Anyone who evades tax is doing something forbidden.
The missing tax must be paid as back tax with interest.
On top of that there is a fine, often as high as the evaded tax.
Declaring honestly pays off.

abschnitte.text: In your **tax return** you have to declare your income and wealth honestly. Anyone who deliberately keeps something quiet, such as income from a side job or a bank account, is committing **tax evasion**. People who act **negligently**, in other words do not take enough care, can also be punished. If no documents are forged, it is called evasion and not fraud.

Taxes pay for schools, roads, the police and much more. If someone deliberately does not pay even though they should, this money is missing. Then the others have to bear more. That is why tax evasion is **forbidden** and **unfair** to everyone who pays honestly.

If the evasion is discovered, you have to pay the missing taxes as **back tax**, plus **default interest**. In addition, there is a **fine**. As a rule, it is as high as the evaded tax. If the fault is minor it can be lower, and if it is serious up to three times as high.

Anyone who reports a mistake themselves before the tax office discovers it is making a **voluntary disclosure**. The first time in your life, you then get off without a fine. However, you still have to pay the back tax and the interest. So it is worth correcting mistakes quickly.

gewusst: Voluntary disclosure without penalty has existed in Switzerland since 2010, but only once in a lifetime.
Heirs can also report tax evasion by the person who has died and so avoid a fine.

teile.einleitung: The vaccination record is a small booklet or a digital list showing all the vaccinations a person has had. This lets you see quickly which diseases you are already protected against and what is still missing.
wichtigste: Every vaccination is entered in the vaccination record with the date.
The name of the vaccine is also entered.
The doctor or another expert enters the vaccination and confirms it.
With the vaccination record you can see which vaccinations are still missing.
You should keep your vaccination record safe all your life.

abschnitte.text: Every vaccination is recorded in the **vaccination record**: the **date**, the name of the vaccine and which disease it protects against. Added to this is a stamp or signature from the surgery that gave the vaccination. Many vaccinations are needed several times so that the protection lasts. The record shows how many doses you have already had.

abschnitte.titel: What do you need it for?
abschnitte.text: The doctor looks in the vaccination record to see which vaccinations from the **Swiss vaccination schedule** are still missing. The vaccination schedule is published by the Confederation’s experts. The record is also important if you are injured: then, for example, they check whether your protection against **tetanus** is still valid. That is why parents are best off bringing it to every visit to the doctor.

For some countries you need certain vaccinations, for example against yellow fever. For this there is the **international certificate of vaccination**, which was introduced by the World Health Organization. When you enter the country, you can use it to show that you have been vaccinated. Anyone planning a big trip should get advice early.

gewusst: The international certificate of vaccination is usually yellow and is therefore often called the “yellow booklet”.
If the vaccination record is lost, the surgery can often enter the vaccinations again from its own records.

teile.einleitung: An ambulance takes sick or injured people to hospital quickly. On board are specially trained paramedics.
wichtigste: On a call-out, the ambulance drives with blue lights and a siren.
Other cars then make way.
Paramedics work in the ambulance.
They look after the person and take them to hospital.
You call an ambulance on the emergency number 144.

abschnitte.text: When an ambulance drives to an emergency, it switches on its **blue lights** and **siren**. You can hear the typical “Tatütata” sound from far away. That way everyone knows that it is urgent. With blue lights, the ambulance may even cross a junction when the light is red, but only carefully.

When you hear the siren, other cars move **to the side** and make way. Cyclists and pedestrians also wait until the ambulance has passed. On the motorway, when there is a traffic jam, people form an **emergency corridor** between the lanes so that the rescue service can get through. In an emergency every minute can be important.

**Paramedics** work in the ambulance. They have done several years of training and know exactly what to do in an emergency. They examine the person, give medicines and treat wounds. In serious emergencies, an **emergency doctor** also comes along. Then they take the person to hospital.

In Switzerland you call the ambulance service on **144**. You say who is calling, where you are and what has happened. Then you stay on the phone and answer the questions. For rescues in the mountains or in places that are hard to reach, there are also helicopters, for example from **Rega**.

gewusst: An ambulance is like a small doctor’s surgery on wheels, with a stretcher, oxygen and equipment for monitoring the heart.
The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Complementary medicine includes treatments that are meant to supplement conventional medicine, for example acupuncture or herbal medicine. In Switzerland, basic insurance pays for five of these methods under certain conditions.
wichtigste: “Complementary” means supplementing.
In 2009, Swiss voters approved a constitutional article on complementary medicine.
Since 2017, basic insurance has permanently paid for five methods.
These include, for example, acupuncture and phytotherapy.
The condition is that the treatment is given by a doctor with recognised further training.
For treatment by therapists who are not doctors, you need supplementary insurance.

abschnitte.text: **Complementary** means supplementing. It refers to treatments that are used alongside **conventional medicine**. These include, for example, **acupuncture** from Chinese medicine, in which fine needles are inserted, or **phytotherapy**, in other words treatment with medicinal plants. Some people swear by them, others are sceptical. The effectiveness of individual methods is debated in science.

In 2009, the people and the cantons in Switzerland approved a new constitutional article on complementary medicine. Since then, the Confederation and the cantons are meant to take it into account. After a trial period, **basic insurance** has permanently paid for five methods since **2017**: acupuncture, anthroposophic medicine, drug therapy of traditional Chinese medicine, classical homeopathy and phytotherapy.

Basic insurance only pays if the treatment is given by a **doctor** who has **recognised further training** in this method. If you go to a therapist who is not a doctor, basic insurance pays nothing. For this you need **supplementary insurance**. It is worth checking with the insurer beforehand.

gewusst: Acupuncture has been known in China for a very long time.
The deductible and excess apply to complementary medicine in exactly the same way as to other treatments.

teile.einleitung: Pocket money is money that children receive regularly from their parents. With it they learn to handle money themselves. You do not have to pay any tax on it.
wichtigste: Pocket money is a gift from your parents and not a wage.
You do not pay income tax on it.
Income from work is taxable, for example an apprentice’s wage.
With pocket money you learn to plan, save and weigh up what you want.
The parents decide how much pocket money a child gets.

abschnitte.text: You pay **income tax** on money that you earn, for example through work. Pocket money is not earnings but a **gift** from your parents within the family. That is why a child does not have to pay tax on it and does not have to fill in a tax return either. This applies throughout Switzerland.

If a child earns money themselves, for example with a **holiday job** or during an apprenticeship, this is **earned income**. This income is taxable in principle. From the year in which you turn 18, you usually fill in your own **tax return**. With small incomes, however, there is often hardly any tax or none at all.

With pocket money you practise making a **budget**. You notice that money can only be spent once. If you save part of it, you can afford something bigger later. Budget advice services give parents guidelines on how much pocket money suits each age.

gewusst: Many parents give younger children pocket money every week and older ones every month.
At many banks you can open a savings account for children very early on.

teile.einleitung: Tax liability means that someone has to pay taxes and submit a tax return. In Switzerland, all adults who live here are liable for tax, even if they have little or no income. Companies are liable for tax too.
wichtigste: Anyone who lives in Switzerland and is an adult is liable for tax.
Even without income you have to submit a tax return.
For the year in which you turn 18, you are liable for tax in your own right.
Your first own tax return arrives in the year after your 18th birthday.
If you live in Switzerland, you declare your worldwide income and wealth.
Double taxation agreements prevent you from paying twice.

abschnitte.titel: Liable in your own right from 18
abschnitte.text: At 18 you are an **adult** and become **liable for tax in your own right**. This already applies to the whole year in which you turn 18. If Jana turns 18 in May 2025, she is liable for tax herself for the tax year 2025. She fills in the tax return for it in 2026. Before that, children are usually taxed together with their parents.

Being liable for tax does not automatically mean that you have to pay a lot. Even people who are studying and have no income have to submit a **tax return**. Elias is 19 and a student: he fills in the tax return too. If he has no income and hardly any wealth, he often has to pay nothing at all or only very little.

Anyone whose **residence** is in Switzerland has **unlimited tax liability**. They have to declare their **entire income and wealth**, including an account or a flat abroad. So that nobody pays twice for the same thing, Switzerland has **double taxation agreements** with many countries. Anyone who only owns a house in Switzerland but lives abroad has **limited tax liability** here.

It is not only people who are liable for tax. Companies such as **public limited companies** and **limited liability companies (GmbH)** pay taxes too, namely on their **profit** and their **capital**. They are called **legal persons**. In tax language, people are called **natural persons**.

gewusst: If a child already earns wages before the age of 18, for example during an apprenticeship, these wages are taxed separately.
In Switzerland, married couples fill in a joint tax return.

teile.einleitung: The deductible is the amount you first pay yourself every year in Swiss basic insurance before the health insurer covers costs. Anyone who chooses a high deductible pays a lower premium in return. Choosing the deductible is therefore a small bet on how healthy you will be in the coming year.
wichtigste: The deductible is a fixed yearly amount that you pay yourself towards doctor’s, medicine and hospital costs.
